docs.title: Parakeet
docs.text:
A data-parallel compiler for numerical Python.

Write ordinary NumPy, loops, comprehensions, or explicit data-parallel operators (map, reduce, scan, allpairs). Parakeet specializes your function for its input types, fuses and tiles the array algebra, and compiles native code for multi-core CPUs, Apple Metal, and NVIDIA CUDA.

Get started Explore the gallery

docs.title: Exact nearest neighbor
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from parakeet import jit


@jit
def nearest(x, y):
  delta = x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :]
  d2 = np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2)
  return np.argmin(d2, axis=1)

Parakeet computes distances a tile at a time on both CPU and GPU, keeping only the winning reference index per tile rather than allocating the full N × M distance matrix. Ties preserve NumPy's first-index rule.

Compare timings and allocations

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
python -m pip install parakeet

Requires Python 3.11+, NumPy 2, and a system C compiler. For GPU backends, install parakeet[metal] on Apple Silicon or parakeet[cuda12] with an NVIDIA GPU.

docs.title: One algebra underneath
docs.text:
Since its beginnings in 2012, Parakeet has been built on a simple observation: most numerical Python — whether written as NumPy expressions, comprehensions, or explicit parallel operators — expresses the same handful of array computations: maps, reductions, scans, filters, and scatters.

@jit
def scaled_tanh_numpy(x, alpha=0.5, beta=0.3):
  return np.tanh(x * alpha) + beta


@jit
def scaled_tanh_comp(x, alpha=0.5, beta=0.3):
  return np.array([np.tanh(xi * alpha) + beta for xi in x])

Both lower to the same single fused parallel loop with no temporary arrays. Keeping that operator algebra intact through the middle end lets a small set of general passes do the heavy lifting:

  • Fusion. Chained array expressions, filtered reductions (np.sum(x[x > 0])), and sibling histograms sharing the same bin IDs merge into one pass. See the tree-split example.
  • Tiling and single-pass reductions. Associative reductions and bilinear products tile into cache or GPU shared memory, so Gaussian kernel regression, nearest-neighbor search, and attention stream blocks instead of allocating giant pairwise matrices. Read the algebraic laws.
  • Gradients. parakeet.grad and parakeet.value_and_grad differentiate the array operators directly, compiling a training step into one native function. Learn about gradients.
  • Inspection. Every stage is visible: inspect the operator IR, see which rewrites fired with parakeet.dsl.show_rewrite, or read the generated C, Metal, or CUDA source. Inspect a rewrite.

docs.title: Algebraic laws
docs.text:
Parakeet started in 2012 with a small algebra of data-parallel operators — maps, reductions, scans, and filters — and a set of fusion and tiling rules over them. Those rules eliminate temporary arrays and improve cache locality for ordinary array expressions, comprehensions, and matrix products.

Many modern numerical and machine-learning kernels need one step further: eliminating quadratic O(N²) or O(M · V) intermediates, turning long serial recurrences into parallel block passes, and avoiding saving giant intermediates for reverse-mode differentiation. Rather than adding special-purpose "layer" ops to the compiler, Parakeet encodes these transformations as six general algebraic laws over the same five operator statements (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, IndexScatter), multi-state Carry folds, and IndexTile / TileStage tiling.

Because the passes match operator algebra instead of model names, the same rules fire on Gaussian kernel regression, shortest-path products, exact nearest-neighbor search, histogram split-finding, and IIR filters as on attention, cross-entropy, and state-space models.

docs.title: The six laws at a glance
docs.text: Law Algebraic idea Middle-end pass Example workloads Law 1 — Rescaled semiring monoids Associative rescaling fold (m₁, l₁, o₁) ⊕ (m₂, l₂, o₂) monoidal tiling Softmax attention, Split-K decoding, linear cross-entropy, Gaussian (RBF) kernel regression, 1-pass logsumexp Law 2 — Algebraic AD rematerialization Sufficient-statistic VJPs that recompute score tiles on the fly algebraic_vjp (in autodiff) Attention backward (no N × N saved), cross-entropy backward (no M × V saved), 1-pass LayerNorm / RMSNorm VJP Law 3 — Bilinear contraction reassociation & shared-KV tiling (U @ Vᵀ) @ Wᵀ = U @ (Vᵀ @ Wᵀ) + folding shared-KV query groups into tiles contraction reassociation Multi-head latent attention absorption, grouped-query attention, low-rank (X @ A) @ B chains Law 4 — Chunkwise state-space duality Affine composition (a₂, b₂) ∘ (a₁, b₁) = (a₂ a₁, a₂ b₁ + b₂) and block duality chunkwise scan Parallel IIR / EMA / Kalman filters, Mamba-2 and gated linear attention recurrences Law 5 — Affine tile-interval pruning Interval bounds [i₀, i₀+Bₘ-1] × [j₀, j₀+Bₙ-1] over index predicates TileInterval in analysis Causal and sliding-window masks, banded matrices, spatial cutoffs, runtime boolean tile skipping Law 6 — Privatized scatter & multi-state carries Commutative/associative scatter-add and ordered multi-field folds IndexScatter, Fold.carries, pairwise fold tiling GBDT histogram splits, exact 1-NN search, argmin/argmax with values, sparse updates

docs.title: Law 1 — Rescaled semiring monoids
docs.text:
Any reduction whose output depends on a global normalizing statistic (a row maximum m, a sum of exponentials l, or a norm) can fuse with a downstream weighted sum in a single tiled pass whenever its running state forms an associative monoid (S, ⊕, e).

For softmax-weighted contractions (attention and Gaussian kernel regression), the state carries the running maximum m, normalizing sum l, and unnormalized output vector o:

m = max(m₁, m₂)
(m₁, l₁, o₁) ⊕ (m₂, l₂, o₂) = (
    m,
    l₁ · exp(m₁ - m) + l₂ · exp(m₂ - m),
    o₁ · exp(m₁ - m) + o₂ · exp(m₂ - m),
)

Because ⊕ is associative, the same monoid covers four workloads without allocating an N × M or M × V matrix:

  1. Tiled softmax attention (flash_monoid): streams tiles of K and V through CPU cache or GPU shared memory against a tile of Q, never materializing the score matrix S or probability matrix P.
  2. Split-K decoding (split_k=True): when the query grid is too small to fill a GPU (for instance, autoregressive decode with small T_q and long T_kv), Parakeet splits T_kv across threadblocks computing partial (mₚ, lₚ, oₚ) summaries and merges them with the same ⊕.
  3. Tiled linear cross-entropy (monoid_lse): tiles H @ W over the vocabulary dimension V using the scalar (m, l) monoid while gathering the target score on the fly, avoiding an M × V logit matrix.
  4. Gaussian / RBF kernel regression (score_op="sqdist"): recognizes -γ · ||xᵢ - yⱼ||² feeding a normalized exponential sum and compiles Nadaraya-Watson smoothing into one O(N + M)-memory kernel.

docs.title: Law 2 — Algebraic rematerialization in reverse-mode AD
docs.text:
A naive reverse-mode tape saves every forward intermediate, which would bring back O(N²) memory for attention and O(M · V) memory for linear cross-entropy. Parakeet's tape optimizer (parakeet/transforms/algebraic_vjp.py) runs at the operator level before lowering and substitutes sufficient-statistic adjoints where an algebraic identity exists:

  • Attention backward (flash_monoid_bwd): saves only (Q, K, V, O, lse) — no N × N tensor is kept. A cheap O(N · D) pass computes Dᵢ = sum_d dO[i, d] · O[i, d], and the tiled backward kernel recomputes each score tile P = exp(S - lse) and dS = P · (dO @ Vᵀ - D) in on-chip memory while accumulating dK and dV.
  • Linear cross-entropy backward (cce_bwd): saves only (H, W, targets, lse) and recomputes tile probabilities p[i, v] = exp(hᵢ · wᵥ - lseᵢ) while accumulating dH and dW.
  • LayerNorm and RMSNorm VJP: collapses multi-pass mean/variance backward graphs into a single pass over the saved normalized output and inverse scale.
  • Standalone softmax VJP: drops the max adjoint completely using dS = P · (dP - sum(P · dP)).

docs.title: Law 3 — Bilinear contraction reassociation & shared-KV tiling
docs.text:
For a chain of two bilinear contractions sharing a single-use intermediate T:

T[u, k] = sum_r U[u, r] · V[k, r]
Y[p, u] = sum_k W[p, k] · T[u, k]

reassociating the summation order computes the same result:

M[p, r] = sum_k W[p, k] · V[k, r]
Y[p, u] = sum_r M[p, r] · U[u, r]

parakeet/transforms/reassociate.py compares the multiply-add counts U·K·(R + P) against P·R·(K + U) and chooses the cheaper order:

  • Latent attention absorption: given K = C_kv @ W_uk, V = C_kv @ W_uv, and O = softmax(Q @ Kᵀ) @ V, Law 3 emits a runtime shape-guarded branch that absorbs W_uk into Q (Q_abs = Q @ W_ukᵀ) and moves W_uv after attention (O = (P @ C_kv) @ W_uv). Because monoidal tiling (Law 1) runs right after Law 3 on both branches, short-query decode runs tiled attention directly over the compressed latent C_kv without materializing expanded K or V, while long-query prefill automatically takes the lower-FLOP expanded branch.
  • Low-rank matrix chains: (X @ A) @ B and X @ (A @ B) pick the lower-FLOP association at runtime, and remain differentiable under grad.
  • Shared-KV head-group tiling: when a batch axis g of Q (size G) does not vary in K or V (grouped-query attention), Parakeet folds g into the query row index (i_eff = g * T_q + i) so all G query heads share one shared-memory load of K and V.

docs.title: Law 4 — Chunkwise state-space duality
docs.text:
A sequential loop of length T has O(T) serial depth and cannot use multiple cores or GPU threadblocks directly. parakeet/transforms/tile_scan.py recognizes two associative recurrence patterns inside plain Python for t in range(T): loops:

  1. Affine recurrences (s[t] = a[t] * s[t - 1] + b[t]): covers exponential moving averages, IIR filters, and scalar Kalman filters. The loop is rewritten into a 3-stage chunkwise scan (chunk size C = 64) using affine composition (a₂, b₂) ∘ (a₁, b₁) = (a₂ a₁, a₂ b₁ + b₂), reducing serial depth by 64× with no O(T) temporary arrays.
  2. Bilinear matrix-state recurrences: 
    for t in range(T):
  S = a[t] * S + k[t][:, None] * v[t][None, :]
  out[t] = q[t] @ S
    Rewritten into a 4-step division-free chunkwise scan (C = 64):
  3. Step 0: parallel cumulative decay products inside each chunk (exact even when a[t] == 0 or a[t] < 0, and when T is not a multiple of C).
  4. Step 1: intra-chunk quadratic attention-form products Y_intra[c] = ((Q[c] @ K[c]ᵀ) * L[c]) @ V[c].
  5. Step 2: chunk state summary B[c] = K_scaled[c]ᵀ @ V[c].
  6. Step 3: 64× shorter inter-chunk recurrence S_in[c + 1] = A[c] * S_in[c] + B[c].
  7. Step 4: off-diagonal readout Y_off[c] = Q[c] @ S_in[c] combined with Y_intra[c].

Because chunkwise scan runs before tiling, the matrix products in Steps 1, 2, and 4 automatically flow into CPU register tiling, Metal simdgroup_matrix, and CUDA nvcuda::wmma Tensor Cores.

docs.title: Law 5 — Affine tile-interval mask pruning
docs.text:
In parakeet/transforms/analysis.py, TileInterval propagates coordinate bounds [i₀, i₀ + B_M - 1] and [j₀, j₀ + B_N - 1] through affine index expressions and boolean connectives:

  • Causal masks (j <= i): proves tiles with j₀ > i₀ + B_M - 1 are entirely false (skipped before loading K or V) and tiles with j₀ + B_N - 1 <= i₀ are entirely true (run through a branchless inner loop).
  • Sliding windows ((j <= i) & (i - j <= W)): skips both future tiles and tiles outside the window, reducing O(N²) work to O(N · W) from ordinary mask code.
  • Runtime boolean masks: when a mask comes from a runtime array, GPU kernels cooperatively check whether any entry in the tile is true and skip empty tiles before loading values.

docs.title: Law 6 — Privatized scatter & multi-state carries
docs.text:
Two patterns show up constantly outside dense linear algebra: accumulating into shared bins (np.bincount, parakeet.scatter_add) and folding structured state (argmin, Welford variance, custom dsl.fold).

  • Keyed histogram fusion: sibling IndexScatter statements sharing the same index expression (such as gradient and Hessian histograms in a decision tree split search) merge into one traversal over the data, lowered with thread-privatized bins on CPU and parallel atomics/privatization on GPU.
  • Ordered multi-state carries and pairwise tile folds: Fold.carries tracks multiple scalar accumulators in one reduction pass while preserving chunk order (so leftmost ties in argmin or non-commutative compositions in dsl.fold stay exact). pairwise fold tiling fuses a pairwise score producer directly into an ordered fold over bounded tiles on both CPU and GPU — eliminating the full N × M distance matrix in both broadcasting NumPy and nested-map 1-NN.

docs.title: Inspecting rewrites with parakeet.dsl
docs.text:
Call parakeet.dsl.show_rewrite on any function to see which laws fired, which tiled plans were selected, and the operator IR before and after the middle-end passes:

import numpy as np
from parakeet import dsl


@dsl.kernel
def causal_attention(q, k, v):
  causal = dsl.imap(lambda i, j: i >= j, (q.shape[0], k.shape[0]))
  s = dsl.where(causal, (q @ k.T) * dsl.f32(0.125), dsl.f32(-1e9))
  e = dsl.exp(s - dsl.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / dsl.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ v


q = np.zeros((128, 64), np.float32)
print(dsl.show_rewrite(causal_attention, q, q, q).summary())

Parakeet Algebraic Rewrite Report for `causal_attention`
  Laws triggered : Law 1: Rescaled Semiring Monoid Tile Fusion, Law 5: Affine Tile-Interval Mask Pruning
  Monoidal plans : flash_monoid
  Operators      : IndexMap 5 -> 1 | IndexTile 1 | IndexScatter 0 -> 0 | Carry folds 0

See the Kernel gallery for runnable examples and timings across all six laws.

docs.title: parakeet.jit
docs.text:
Compile a numerical Python function to native code on first call.

Use it bare (@jit) or with options (@jit(backend="metal")). The function is specialised for each distinct combination of argument types; every later call with the same types runs the cached native code.

Options (all default to the corresponding parakeet.config setting):

backend "auto", "c", "multicore", "threads", "openmp", "gcd", "metal"/"mps", "cuda" or "python". bounds_check Raise IndexError for out-of-range indices instead of crashing. fusion Fuse array expressions into single loops. tiling Tile matmul-shaped loops for cache locality.

docs.title: parakeet.DeviceArray
docs.text:
An array resident on a GPU device (Metal or CUDA) across @jit calls.

Created with :func:parakeet.to_device or returned automatically by a @jit function called with DeviceArray inputs. Passing a DeviceArray into subsequent @jit calls on the same device avoids redundant host-to-device uploads, and GPU-computed outputs are promoted directly to DeviceArray without device-to-host downloads — keeping weights, gradients, and optimizer state resident on the GPU throughout a training loop.

Call :meth:numpy or :func:parakeet.to_host (or np.asarray(da)) to bring the contents back to host memory.

docs.title: parakeet.dsl.fold(el, lift, merge, x, init=None, *, axis=None, indexed=False, emit=None)
docs.text:
Lift elements to scalar/fixed-vector tuple states and merge adjacent states in input order.

With no axis, lift each leading slice and return one state. With an axis, fold the lanes along that axis and project each state with emit (which may return a scalar, a fixed-size array, or a tuple/NamedTuple of them). An indexed lift receives (value, index) with the index local to its lane. A supplied seed is applied once on the left; an unseeded empty fold raises.

docs.title: parakeet.errors
docs.text:
Exception hierarchy.

Compile-time problems are reported as :class:CompileError subclasses that carry the location of the offending Python source, so the message points at the user's code rather than at Parakeet internals. Runtime problems detected by generated code (out-of-bounds indices, shape mismatches, ...) are re-raised as the same built-in exception NumPy/Python would have raised.

docs.title: Gradients
docs.text:
grad turns a function into its gradient. It is an adverb like map and reduce: it is applied while your code is compiled, and what comes out is ordinary loops that are fused, tiled and run in parallel like everything else.

import numpy as np
from parakeet import grad, value_and_grad


def loss(w, x, y):
  return np.mean((np.tanh(x @ w) - y) ** 2)


g = grad(loss)(w, x, y)  # d loss / d w, shaped like w
value, g = value_and_grad(loss)(w, x, y)
gw, gx = grad(loss, (0, 1))(w, x, y)  # several arguments at once

The function has to return one floating point number. The arguments you differentiate with respect to can be floats, float arrays, or tuples of those nested however you like — the gradient comes back with the same structure:

def mlp(params, x, y):
  (w1, b1), (w2, b2) = params
  h = np.tanh(x @ w1 + b1)
  return np.mean((h @ w2 + b2 - y) ** 2)


(gw1, gb1), (gw2, gb2) = grad(mlp)(params, x, y)

grad(f) can be called from plain Python, where it compiles on first use, or inside a @jit function, where the whole training step becomes one compiled function:

@jit
def descend(w, x, y, rate, steps):
  for _ in range(steps):
    w = w - rate * grad(loss)(w, x, y)
  return w

examples/nanogpt.py trains a small transformer this way, and examples/convnet.py a convolutional network.

docs.title: What can be differentiated
docs.text:
arithmetic and math functions + - * / **, np.exp, np.tanh, np.maximum, np.where, np.abs, np.clip, … with broadcasting reductions np.sum, np.mean, np.var, np.std, np.max, np.min, np.prod, np.linalg.norm, with axis and keepdims; parakeet.reduce with add, multiply, minimum, maximum linear algebra @, np.dot, np.matmul for vectors, matrices and stacks of matrices; np.einsum running and ordered np.cumsum, parakeet.scan(add, x), np.sort folds parakeet.reduce(f, x) with any function f views slicing, x.T, reshape, ravel, np.transpose, x[:, None] indexing with arrays x[idx], x[rows, cols] building arrays np.concatenate, np.stack, np.array([a, b, c]), comprehensions adverbs map/each, allpairs, imap with your own functions, including functions that use arrays from outside scalar code anything written with scalars, conditional expressions included

Derivatives of min, max, abs and friends at a tie follow the usual conventions: ties in a reduction share the gradient equally.

docs.title: Loops and branches
docs.text:
The derivative is laid out when the function is compiled, so the compiler has to know how many times each operation runs.

A for loop over a tuple, or over a range whose length is known when the function is compiled, is unrolled: a literal, a scalar argument, or the shape of an array all work. Such an argument becomes part of what the function is specialized on, exactly like axis=.

def deep(weights, x):  # a tuple of matrices
  for w in weights:
    x = np.tanh(x @ w)
  return np.sum(x)


def correlate(x, kernel):
  out = x[: len(x) - len(kernel) + 1] * 0.0
  for i in range(len(kernel)):  # unrolled: one specialization per kernel length
    out = out + x[i : i + len(out)] * kernel[i]
  return np.sum(out**2)

Loops that do not touch differentiated values are left alone, so a training loop around grad is an ordinary loop.

What cannot be unrolled cannot be differentiated: while loops, loops over the elements of an array of unknown length, and anything longer than 4096 iterations. Use an array operation or an adverb instead — np.sum, parakeet.map, a comprehension.

An if statement whose condition is only known at run time is differentiated by running both branches and choosing between their results, which is what np.where does. That is only possible when running the branch not taken has no effect, so the branches may only assign variables: no return, raise, break, no stores into arrays, no in-place updates. Remember that both sides are computed: if x > 0: y = np.log(x) evaluates the logarithm either way.

if np.sum(x) > 10.0:  # fine
  h, scale = np.tanh(h), 2.0
else:
  h, scale = h * h, 3.0

A guard that only raises (if n == 0: raise ValueError(...)) is fine too, and is not run for both sides.

docs.title: Writing into arrays
docs.text:
Stores are differentiated: assigning a slice, an element, or updating in place all work, in straight-line code and in loops that can be unrolled.

out = np.zeros((n, 3))
out[:3] = x[:3] @ w
out[3:] = np.tanh(x[3:] @ w)
out += bias

Going backwards, whatever adjoint arrived for the stored region belongs to the value that was stored, and the region starts again from zero.

One thing cannot work: overwriting a value that an earlier operation's derivative still has to read. y = np.tanh(h); h[0] = 5.0 is refused, because the derivative of tanh needs the old h; y = np.sum(h * 3.0); h[0] = 5.0 is fine, because that derivative does not. Stores through an array of indices (out[idx] = v) are not differentiated.

docs.title: The gradient is right or there is none
docs.text:
Parakeet never returns a gradient that silently ignores part of your function. If something on the way from the arguments to the result has no derivative rule — np.cumprod, np.convolve, a scan with your own function — you get an UnsupportedError naming it:

UnsupportedError: cannot differentiate through cumprod() (line 12): its derivative is not implemented

docs.title: Second derivatives
docs.text:
grad of a function that calls grad works for element-wise operators, reductions, matrix products and views — enough for gradient penalties and Hessian-vector products:

def penalty(w, x):
  g = grad(loss)(w, x)  # the gradient, as part of the function
  return np.sum(g * g)


grad(penalty)(w, x)  # 2 H g, reverse over reverse

It is refused, by name, through map with your own function, indexing with arrays, cumsum, sort, folds and np.stack/np.concatenate.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
A gradient costs about two to three times the function. Element-wise chains are fused in both directions; a matrix product's derivative is two more matrix products.

The derivative of map/allpairs with your own function runs in parallel like the map itself. Every element may add to the gradient of an array the function captured (the weights of a network mapped over a batch), so each chunk of the loop adds to a copy of its own and the copies are summed at the end: a reduction whose accumulator is the whole gradient. That costs memory: one copy of the captured parameters per thread, up to 256 MB, beyond which fewer chunks are used.

Loops are unrolled, so a long unrolled loop makes for a long compile.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
While the function is elaborated, a tape records each array operator applied to a value that depends on the differentiated arguments. The record is made where the operator still has its algebraic meaning, so each rule is one line: an element-wise operator becomes a map of the scalar function's partial derivative, a sum broadcasts its adjoint back, a matrix product becomes two more, a map differentiates its function again per element.

Scalars are not recorded. An expression in Parakeet's IR is already a record of how it was computed, so the adjoint of a scalar is pushed straight down its expression tree. Views are not recorded either: a slice of an array is the same slice of its adjoint.

See parakeet/transforms/autodiff.py.

docs.title: Backends and GPUs
docs.text:
Every backend runs the same compiled host program (C). They differ in how the parallel loops inside it are executed.

backend Parallel loops run on Notes "auto" the best multi-core strategy found default; same as "multicore" "c" the calling thread no threads at all; also compiles without parallel loop overhead "threads" Parakeet's persistent thread pool POSIX; fork-safe; no extra runtime library "gcd" Grand Central Dispatch macOS "openmp" the compiler's OpenMP runtime needs libgomp/libomp (macOS: brew install libomp) "metal" / "mps" the Apple GPU pip install "parakeet[metal]==1.0.0" "cuda" an NVIDIA GPU pip install "parakeet[cuda12]==1.0.0" (CuPy) "python" — runs the original function uncompiled 
parakeet.available_backends()
# {'python': 'ok', 'c': 'ok', 'threads': 'ok', 'gcd': 'ok', 'openmp': 'ok', 'metal': 'ok',
#  'cuda': 'unavailable: the CUDA backend needs CuPy, which is not installed. Install ...'}

A backend that cannot work fails when you select it, with a message saying what is missing and how to install it — not later with a linker error.

docs.title: Multi-core
docs.text:
Array expressions, map/allpairs/imap, comprehensions, parfor and reductions over recognised associative operations are split into chunks that run on parakeet.config.num_threads threads (default: all cores). Only the outermost data-parallel operation is parallelised; anything nested inside it runs sequentially within each thread.

Small loops are not worth a thread hand-off: loops with a cheap body run on the calling thread unless they have at least 2 * config.parallel_grain iterations (default 8192 per chunk). Loops whose body contains loops of its own are always split.

Compiled functions release the GIL and are safe to call from several Python threads at once. With multiprocessing, prefer the spawn start method when using "openmp" or "gcd" (those runtimes do not survive fork); the default thread pool does.

docs.title: Apple GPUs (Metal)
docs.text:
@jit(backend="metal")
def blur_energy(img):
  return (img[1:-1, 1:-1] * 4 - img[:-2, 1:-1] - img[2:, 1:-1] - img[1:-1, :-2] - img[1:-1, 2:]) ** 2

Each eligible parallel loop is also compiled to a Metal compute kernel; the host program hands loops of at least config.device_threshold iterations (default 32768) to the GPU and runs smaller ones on the CPU.

Apple GPUs have no float64

Metal does not support double precision. A loop that touches float64 data runs on the CPU thread pool instead, and Parakeet emits a FallbackWarning saying so. Pass float32 arrays and np.float32 scalars to stay on the GPU (a Python float argument is a double; x * 2.0 with a literal is fine).

Other reasons a loop stays on the CPU: it allocates temporary arrays per iteration, or it uses a function Metal lacks (lgamma, erfc). The warning always names the reason. Control this with config.device_fallback: "warn" (default), "silent", or "error" to refuse instead.

Runtime errors inside kernels (out-of-bounds indices, failed assertions) are reported as normal Python exceptions.

docs.title: NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA)
docs.text:
@jit(backend="cuda")
def distances(X, C):
  return parakeet.allpairs(lambda a, b: np.sum((a - b) ** 2), X, C)

Kernels are compiled at run time by CuPy's RawKernel (NVRTC), so only the NVIDIA driver and a CuPy wheel matching your CUDA version are needed. All dtypes including float64 are supported. The same per-loop fallback rules apply.

Validation status

CI has no NVIDIA hardware, so there the CUDA code generator runs against a simulator (PARAKEET_CUDA_SIMULATE=1) that compiles the generated kernels as C++ and executes their thread grid on the CPU.

The 1.0 release comparison ran on a physical NVIDIA A10 with strict device dispatch. Earlier checks on an A100 (Google Colab, CuPy with CUDA 13, Python 3.13) and Tesla T4 covered the whole test suite with every parallel loop forced onto the GPU (688 tests, including the tiled products, the gradient tests and arrays kept on the device between loops), the examples and the benchmarks all passed. That check is run on demand, not by CI:

pip install runplz google-colab-cli
runplz colab tools/colab_job.py          # T4; PK_COLAB_GPU=A100 for others

To push your own test suite through a GPU set PARAKEET_TEST_BACKENDS=cuda (the backends used by parakeet.testing.expect and check) and PARAKEET_DEVICE_THRESHOLD=1 (so small arrays go to the device too).

docs.title: What about TPUs?
docs.text: No. A TPU only runs programs compiled by XLA, which wants whole-array operations with static shapes; Parakeet generates scalar loops in C-like kernel languages. Parakeet's CPU backends do work on a Colab TPU host (24 x86 cores), which is all PK_COLAB_TPU=v5e1 runplz colab tools/colab_job.py checks.

docs.title: How data moves
docs.text:
Arrays belong to the host, but within one call they stay on the device.

  • The first GPU loop that uses an array puts it on the device. A buffer the host allocated and has not written to yet (the output of the loop, usually) is created there directly: nothing is copied. On Metal, arrays allocated by compiled code are shared with the GPU without copying at all.
  • Later loops find the array already there. What a loop wrote stays on the device; it is not copied back after every loop.
  • Host code that reads or writes array memory itself (an explicit Python loop, a loop that fell back to the CPU, a call into the BLAS) first asks for everything the device has changed. So does the end of the call.
  • A temporary that is freed before anyone on the host looked at it is never copied back.

A chain of array operations on a GPU therefore costs one upload of its inputs and one download of its result, however many loops it has. Mixing GPU loops with scalar host loops over the same arrays works, and gives the same answers, but pays for a download and an upload each time the two alternate.

Which loops go to the device. A loop is sent when its number of elements times the estimated inner iterations per element reaches config.device_threshold, and it has at least 1024 elements. A loop over 5,000 rows that each need a 10,000-step inner loop goes; a loop over 20,000 cheap elements stays on the CPU, where the launch would cost more than the work; so does a loop over 32 features however long each one's scan is, because a device runs one (slow) thread per element and 32 of them are no match for a few CPU cores.

Use parakeet.to_device(x, backend="cuda") or backend="metal" to reuse resident array inputs across calls. Pass the resulting device arrays to a compiled function and call parakeet.to_host(result) when Python needs the data. Operations which run on the host can still require transfers.

docs.title: Bioinformatics & structural biology
docs.text:
Scientific computing in genomics, cheminformatics, and structural biology is full of kernels that do not fit standard dense GEMM libraries: byte-level FASTQ parsing and 2-bit k-mer packing, multi-channel alignment pileups, 2048-bit chemical fingerprint screening, 3D protein coordinate message passing, and banded dynamic programming alignments.

Parakeet compiles these workloads directly from concise NumPy and data-parallel operators into fused, multi-core CPU and GPU code — without hand-writing C, CUDA, or Metal.

Every snippet below is included from examples/bio_gallery.py. Run the gallery checks or reproducible benchmarks from a source checkout:

python -m examples.bio_gallery
python benchmarks/bio_workloads.py

docs.title: How algebraic primitives map to bio workloads
docs.text: Domain task Algebraic operator / law in Parakeet What the compiler eliminates FASTQ k-mers & read QC parfor + uint8 / uint64 bitwise arithmetic Python per-character loops and string copies Multi-channel BAM pileup Keyed IndexScatter fusion Redundant passes over alignment positions (6 -> 1) Chemical fingerprint screening allpairs + ordered dsl.fold (pairwise_fold) O(N · M) similarity matrix allocation 3D protein RBF / equivariant attention Law 1 rescaled-monoid tiling (flash_monoid) + grad O(N²) pairwise distance & weight matrices Banded Smith-Waterman & genome SSMs Two-row banded DP + Law 4 TileScan Python DP interpreter overhead & sequential scan bottlenecks

docs.title: 1. FASTQ 2-bit canonical k-mers and read QC
docs.text:
Representing raw DNA and Phred quality bytes as uint8 arrays lets Parakeet compute forward and reverse-complement 2-bit uint64 canonical k-mers (min(fwd, revcomp)), GC fraction, and mean Phred quality in one parallel pass over reads:

@parakeet.jit
def encode_canonical_kmers_and_gc(seq_bytes, qual_bytes, k):
  """Encode a batch of equal-length ASCII DNA reads (N, L) uint8 into:
  - canonical 2-bit k-mers (N, L - k + 1) uint64  [min(fwd, revcomp)]
  - per-read GC fraction (N,) float32
  - per-read mean Phred quality (N,) float32
  """
  n_reads, read_len = seq_bytes.shape
  n_kmers = read_len - k + 1
  kmers = np.empty((n_reads, n_kmers), dtype=np.uint64)
  gc_frac = np.empty((n_reads,), dtype=np.float32)
  mean_q = np.empty((n_reads,), dtype=np.float32)
  mask = (~np.uint64(0)) >> np.uint64(64 - 2 * k)
  rev_shift = np.uint64(2 * (k - 1))

  def process_read(r):
    gc = np.int64(0)
    qsum = np.int64(0)
    fwd = np.uint64(0)
    rev = np.uint64(0)
    for pos in range(read_len):
      ch = seq_bytes[r, pos]
      # ASCII: A=65 -> 0, C=67 -> 1, G=71 -> 2, T=84 -> 3
      is_c = ch == np.uint8(67)
      is_g = ch == np.uint8(71)
      is_t = ch == np.uint8(84)
      code = np.uint64(1) if is_c else (np.uint64(2) if is_g else (np.uint64(3) if is_t else np.uint64(0)))
      comp = np.uint64(3) ^ code
      if is_c or is_g:
        gc = gc + np.int64(1)
      qsum = qsum + np.int64(qual_bytes[r, pos]) - np.int64(33)
      fwd = ((fwd << np.uint64(2)) | code) & mask
      rev = (rev >> np.uint64(2)) | (comp << rev_shift)
      if pos >= k - 1:
        kmers[r, pos - k + 1] = fwd if fwd < rev else rev
    gc_frac[r] = np.float32(gc) / np.float32(read_len)
    mean_q[r] = np.float32(qsum) / np.float32(read_len)

  parakeet.parfor(process_read, n_reads)
  return kmers, gc_frac, mean_q

docs.title: 2. Single-pass multi-channel alignment pileup
docs.text:
A pileup records A/C/G/T base counts, Phred quality sums, and reverse-strand counts at each reference coordinate. Because all six parakeet.scatter_add updates share the same index array ref_pos, Parakeet's scatter-fusion pass combines them into a single privatized traversal (IndexScatter: 6 -> 1):

@parakeet.jit
def single_pass_pileup(ref_pos, base_code, phred_q, is_rev, contig_len):
  """Accumulate A/C/G/T counts, quality sums, and reverse-strand counts across
  aligned base observations in one keyed IndexScatter traversal."""
  is_a = (base_code == np.uint8(0)).astype(np.int64)
  is_c = (base_code == np.uint8(1)).astype(np.int64)
  is_g = (base_code == np.uint8(2)).astype(np.int64)
  is_t = (base_code == np.uint8(3)).astype(np.int64)
  q_i64 = phred_q.astype(np.int64)
  rev_i64 = is_rev.astype(np.int64)

  # All six histograms share `ref_pos` -> Parakeet fuses them into ONE traversal!
  cnt_a = parakeet.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, is_a)
  cnt_c = parakeet.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, is_c)
  cnt_g = parakeet.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, is_g)
  cnt_t = parakeet.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, is_t)
  qual_sum = parakeet.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, q_i64)
  rev_cnt = parakeet.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, rev_i64)
  return cnt_a, cnt_c, cnt_g, cnt_t, qual_sum, rev_cnt

docs.title: 3. 2048-bit Morgan fingerprint Tanimoto screening
docs.text:
Chemical similarity screening compares query fingerprints (N, 32) against a compound library (M, 32) of packed uint64 bitvectors (2,048 bits each). Combining a portable 64-bit SWAR popcount with dsl.allpairs and an ordered dsl.fold finds the closest library compound per query while preserving first-index ties:

def popcount64(x):
  """Branchless 64-bit SWAR popcount (portable across C, multicore, Metal, CUDA)."""
  u = x - ((x >> np.uint64(1)) & np.uint64(0x5555555555555555))
  u = (u & np.uint64(0x3333333333333333)) + ((u >> np.uint64(2)) & np.uint64(0x3333333333333333))
  u = (u + (u >> np.uint64(4))) & np.uint64(0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F)
  return (u * np.uint64(0x0101010101010101)) >> np.uint64(56)


class BestHit(NamedTuple):
  sim: np.float32
  index: np.int64


def better_hit(left, right):
  # Highest Tanimoto similarity wins; ties preserve the first library compound.
  return right if right.sim > left.sim else left


@parakeet.jit
def tanimoto_nearest_hit(queries, library):
  """Find the closest library compound per query over packed uint64 fingerprints
  (N, W) x (M, W) using tiled pairwise folds with zero N x M allocation."""
  pop_q = np.sum(popcount64(queries), axis=1)
  pop_l = np.sum(popcount64(library), axis=1)

  def inter_bits(q_row, l_row):
    return np.sum(popcount64(q_row & l_row))

  # Stream intersection counts into an ordered fold over library compounds
  inter = dsl.allpairs(inter_bits, queries, library)
  denom = pop_q[:, None] + pop_l[None, :] - inter
  sim = np.where(
    denom > np.uint64(0), inter.astype(np.float32) / np.maximum(denom, np.uint64(1)).astype(np.float32), np.float32(0.0)
  )
  return dsl.fold(
    lambda score, ref_idx: BestHit(score, ref_idx),
    better_hit,
    sim,
    axis=1,
    indexed=True,
    emit=lambda hit: hit.index,
  )

docs.title: 4. 3D protein coordinate RBF message passing
docs.text:
Pairwise radial-basis-function smoothing over 3D residue coordinates (N, 3) uses the same rescaled-monoid structure as softmax attention. Law 1 fuses the squared-distance computation, softmax normalization, and feature aggregation into a single tiled pass with zero O(N²) score allocation — and parakeet.grad differentiates through the 3D coordinates directly:

@parakeet.jit
def protein_rbf_message_passing(coords, features, neg_inv_2sigma2):
  """3D radial-basis-function message passing over residue coordinates (N, 3).

  Fuses into Law 1 online (m, l, O) monoidal tiles with zero N x N materialization.
  """
  d2 = np.sum((coords[:, None, :] - coords[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2.0), axis=-1)
  s = d2 * neg_inv_2sigma2
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ features


def protein_rbf_loss(coords, features, targets, neg_inv_2sigma2):
  pred = protein_rbf_message_passing(coords, features, neg_inv_2sigma2)
  diff = pred - targets
  return np.mean(diff * diff)


protein_coord_grad = parakeet.grad(protein_rbf_loss, argnum=0)

docs.title: 5. Banded Smith-Waterman alignment and DNA state-space scan
docs.text:
Compiled two-row banded Smith-Waterman keeps only O(M) score scratch in L1 cache, while 1D DNA exponential state-space recurrences automatically rewrite into Law 4 chunkwise parallel affine prefix scans (TileScan):

@parakeet.jit
def banded_smith_waterman(seq_a, seq_b, match_score, mismatch_pen, gap_pen, band_width):
  """Banded Smith-Waterman local alignment score over integer-encoded sequences.

  Keeps only two O(M) score rows in cache and restricts columns to |j - i| <= band_width.
  """
  n = seq_a.shape[0]
  m = seq_b.shape[0]
  prev = np.zeros((m + 1,), dtype=np.float32)
  curr = np.zeros((m + 1,), dtype=np.float32)
  best = np.float32(0.0)
  for i in range(1, n + 1):
    ai = seq_a[i - 1]
    j_lo = i - band_width
    if j_lo < 1:
      j_lo = 1
    j_hi = i + band_width
    if j_hi > m:
      j_hi = m
    for j in range(j_lo, j_hi + 1):
      sub = match_score if ai == seq_b[j - 1] else mismatch_pen
      v = prev[j - 1] + sub
      up = prev[j] + gap_pen
      left = curr[j - 1] + gap_pen
      if up > v:
        v = up
      if left > v:
        v = left
      if v < np.float32(0.0):
        v = np.float32(0.0)
      curr[j] = v
      if v > best:
        best = v
    for j in range(j_lo, j_hi + 1):
      prev[j] = curr[j]
      curr[j] = np.float32(0.0)
  return best


@parakeet.jit
def dna_ssm_scan(decay, signal):
  """Exponential state-space scan along a DNA track (L,).

  Compiled via Law 4 chunkwise parallel affine prefix scan (TileScan).
  """
  length = decay.shape[0]
  out = np.empty_like(signal)
  s = np.float32(0.0)
  for t in range(length):
    s = decay[t] * s + signal[t]
    out[t] = s
  return out

docs.text:

docs.title: 1.0.0 (November 24, 2026)
docs.text: A ground-up rewrite for modern Python. The @jit decorator, the adverbs (map, reduce, scan, allpairs, imap, ...) and the overall idea are unchanged; everything underneath is new.

docs.title: Algebraic operators
docs.text:
• The same CPU tile schedule serves exact nearest-neighbor queries written as broadcasting NumPy or nested parallel maps. It merges a distance and index per query and preserves the first index on ties.
  • Two weighted histograms over shared bin IDs can fuse into a single traversal. Structured folds accept tuples and named records with a user-defined merge.
  • Algebraic rewrites cover online normalized sums, their gradients, reassociation of contractions, and chunked affine scans. The rewrite inspector shows which passes fired for a given function and input.
  • The gallery includes runnable examples. The release benchmarks compare five workloads with general-purpose and specialist implementations on a four-vCPU worker and an NVIDIA A10.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• grad and value_and_grad: reverse-mode differentiation as an adverb. Element-wise operators, reductions, matrix products, views, map and allpairs with your own functions all have derivative rules; loops of known length are unrolled; anything without a rule raises instead of returning a wrong gradient. examples/nanogpt.py and examples/convnet.py train with it.
  • More of grad: cumsum, sort, einsum, stacks of matrices, folds with any function, and if statements on run-time conditions (both branches run, results are selected). The derivative of a map runs in parallel.
  • A middle end: elaboration now produces operator statements (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, printed by spec.operators) and a pipeline of passes rewrites them before they become loops. Tiling is one such pass, a pattern match on the IR instead of a trial elaboration; vertical fusion (Map→Map including matmul epilogues, Scan→Map into emit, Map→Filter, Map→Reduce), filter fusion (Filter→Filter and Filter→Reduce: np.sum(x[x > 0]) is one loop and allocates nothing), sibling fusion (x.min(), x.max() and np.sin(x), np.cos(x) each share one loop), reduction interchange (np.sum(X, axis=0) becomes L1-tiled contiguous SIMD loops), and dead-operator elimination all run at this level; find_broken_transform bisects the pass list; config.skip_transforms switches passes off.
  • General operators: reduce, scan and filter take several arrays with map= (and emit=); np.einsum; @ on stacks; reductions over several axes in one pass; tiling for maps of any rank.
  • Parallel primitives: prefix scans (cumsum), filters (x[mask], nonzero) and argmin/argmax run in parallel, on CPUs and GPUs.
  • GPU: arrays stay on the device between the loops of one call; a loop is sent to the device by the work in it, not its element count.
  • BLAS: float matrix products call the BLAS NumPy uses.
  • Tiling: two-dimensional maps of reductions (@, allpairs distances, ...) run a cache-sized tile at a time with their reductions jammed 2×4. A 1024×1024 matrix product is 2× faster on one core and 3× on all of them.
  • np.sort and np.argsort take axis and sort every lane in parallel (N-d input used to be flattened without saying so).
  • The dimensions of an array argument can be compile-time constants when the code needs them to be (range(w.shape[0]) in a loop that must be unrolled).
  • parakeet.macro and parakeet.find_broken_transform are back, and the code is laid out in frontend/, syntax/, transforms/ and lib/ again.
  • Faster compiles for large functions: identical loop bodies are compiled once.
  • Checked on real NVIDIA hardware. The whole suite passes with every parallel loop forced onto a Tesla T4 (tools/colab_job.py, run on demand with runplz colab; not part of CI).
  • Reads like Parakeet again: two-space indentation, parakeet.prims and parakeet.ndtypes, and the 0.x helpers typed_repr, specialize, run_python_fn, openmp_available, rank/size/shape, plus the old config.opt_fusion / config.print_* option names.

  • Fixed: two arguments of one GPU kernel that view the same memory now share a device buffer (previously one of them could read a truncated copy).

  • Python 3.11+ and NumPy 2, no dependencies besides NumPy and a C compiler (the dsltools, appdirs, llvmpy and PyCUDA dependencies are gone).

  • New frontend. Functions are elaborated directly into a typed loop IR: calls are inlined, closures/tuples/slices are resolved at compile time, and array expressions are fused into their consumers.
  • Backends: sequential C; multi-core through a built-in thread pool, OpenMP or Grand Central Dispatch; Apple GPUs through Metal; NVIDIA GPUs through CUDA (CuPy/NVRTC, no nvcc needed). GPU backends fall back to the CPU per loop, with a warning that says why.
  • NumPy-exact typing (NEP 50): result dtypes match NumPy, including the treatment of Python scalars.
  • Safety: bounds checks, shape checks, division and domain checks raise the same exceptions NumPy/Python would; compile errors carry the source location and the chain of inlined calls; reference-counted temporaries are freed eagerly (no more leaks in loops).
  • Much larger language subset: early return, break/continue, while, keyword/default/*args arguments, walrus, assert/raise, boolean-mask and integer-array indexing (reads and writes), in-place operators with NumPy aliasing semantics, 0-d and empty arrays, all integer/float dtypes.
  • Much larger library: ~200 NumPy functions and methods, np.random (a counter-based generator that is reproducible in parallel and on GPUs), sorting, math, and most numeric builtins.

docs.title: Compile-time errors
docs.text:
Everything Parakeet cannot compile is reported when the function is first called with a given set of argument types, as a subclass of parakeet.CompileError:

Exception Meaning UnsupportedError a Python or NumPy feature outside the supported subset TypeInferenceError (also a TypeError) types that cannot be reconciled, wrong arguments StaticValueError (also a ValueError) something that must be a compile-time constant is not, or is invalid

The message carries the source line, a caret under the offending expression, and — because calls are inlined — the chain of calls that led there:

parakeet.errors.TypeInferenceError: indices must be a scalar, got str 'a'
  File "model.py", line 15, in helper
    return v[k] * 2
           ^^^^
called from
  File "model.py", line 21, in outer
    total += helper(x, "a")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

err.location and err.call_chain give the same information programmatically, and a note records the argument types being compiled.

docs.title: Run-time errors
docs.text:
Generated code raises ordinary exceptions, with a note pointing at the source line that failed:

@jit
def third(x):
  return x[2]


third(np.zeros(2))
# IndexError: index 2 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 2
#   raised by compiled code at demo.py:5 (in third)
Situation Exception index out of range IndexError shapes that do not broadcast, bad reshape, ragged map results, empty reduction without identity ValueError //, % or / by zero on Python numbers ZeroDivisionError assert AssertionError allocation failure MemoryError writing to a read-only array ValueError

Checks are also performed inside parallel loops and GPU kernels. When an error occurs, temporaries allocated so far are released.

NumPy array arithmetic follows NumPy: integer division by zero yields 0 and floating-point operations yield inf/nan rather than raising.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
backend="python" : Run the original function. If the answer is still wrong the bug is in your code, not in the compiler: f(x, _backend="python").

f.specialize(*args) : Compile for example arguments without running and return a Specialization: .operators (maps and reductions over index spaces, as elaborated), .ir (typed loop IR after the passes), .source (C), .kernels (GPU kernel sources), .signature.

f.inspect(*args) : Print the IR.

parakeet.config.print_ir, parakeet.config.print_code : Print the IR / C of everything as it is compiled (also PARAKEET_PRINT_IR=1).

@jit(fusion=False) : Evaluate every array expression into its own temporary. Useful to check whether a problem is related to loop fusion.

parakeet.find_broken_transform(fn, inputs) : Switch the optimizations on one at a time — fusion, each pass of the middle end (dead code, vertical fusion, filter fusion, sibling fusion, reduction interchange, tiling), the C optimizer, parallel loops, the GPU — and name the first one that makes the result differ from plain Python (or from expected, if given).

parakeet.clear_cache() : Delete cached compiled modules (they are keyed by the generated source and compiler, so this is never needed for correctness).

If you hit a parakeet.errors.InternalError or a CCompilerError, that is a bug in Parakeet: the message includes where the generated source was kept. Please open an issue with it.

docs.title: Kernel gallery
docs.text:
Parakeet gives you two clean, self-contained ways to write compiled kernels over the same algebraic IR:

  1. NumPy frontend (@parakeet.jit + np.*): Write ordinary NumPy broadcasting, reductions, and matrix products.
  2. Explicit DSL (@dsl.kernel + dsl.*): Write data-parallel kernels directly using dsl.map, dsl.allpairs, dsl.fold, dsl.imap, dsl.ireduce, dsl.scatter, and dsl.* primitives (dsl.min, dsl.sum, dsl.argmin, dsl.isnan, dsl.f32, ...) — no np.* or top-level parakeet.* syntax required.

Start with one nearest-neighbor query comparing both frontends side by side, then change what the fold remembers. For a complete end-to-end training script, try nanoGPT. Every snippet below is included directly from runnable repository examples (python -m examples.algebraic_gallery).

# NumPy frontend:
import numpy as np
import parakeet

# Explicit DSL frontend (self-contained — no numpy needed inside @dsl.kernel):
from typing import NamedTuple
from parakeet import dsl

The same @parakeet.jit decorator compiles both ordinary NumPy and explicit operators such as dsl.map, dsl.allpairs, dsl.imap, dsl.ireduce, dsl.iscatter, and dsl.fold (dsl.kernel is an alias for parakeet.jit). Browse the source.

The axis-fold examples below use the development version after 1.0.0. To run them, install the current checkout with python -m pip install -e ..

docs.title: Exact nearest neighbor
docs.text:
Given Q query rows and R reference rows with the same feature count, return the index of the closest reference to each query. For a query at 1 and references at 0, 2, and 4, the squared distances are [1, 1, 9], so the answer is index 0 because ties keep the earlier index (and the first NaN wins, matching NumPy).

Broadcasting NumPyMap and argminAll pairs and a structured fold 
@parakeet.jit
def nearest_numpy(queries, references):
  delta = queries[:, None, :] - references[None, :, :]
  return np.argmin(np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2), axis=1)

For each query, map the same distance function over the references and return the position of its smallest value. The outer map repeats that search for every query.

def squared_distance(query, reference):
  return dsl.sum((query - reference) ** dsl.f32(2))



@dsl.kernel
def exact_1nn(x_query, x_ref):
  """Exact nearest-neighbor index per query row."""
  return dsl.map(
    lambda query: dsl.argmin(dsl.map(lambda reference: squared_distance(query, reference), x_ref)),
    x_query,
  )

def squared_distance(query, reference):
  return dsl.sum((query - reference) ** dsl.f32(2))



class Winner(NamedTuple):
  distance: dsl.f32
  index: dsl.i64


def first_minimum(left, right):
  # Keep the first NaN. Among finite values, replace only on strict improvement.
  right_wins = dsl.isnan(right.distance) or right.distance < left.distance
  return right if right_wins and not dsl.isnan(left.distance) else left


@dsl.kernel
def nearest_fold(queries, references):
  scores = dsl.allpairs(squared_distance, queries, references)
  return dsl.fold(Winner, first_minimum, scores, axis=1, indexed=True, emit=lambda winner: winner.index)

In nearest_fold, allpairs defines the logical Q × R domain of squared distances, Winner pairs each distance with its reference index, and first_minimum merges adjacent winners while keeping left ties and the first NaN. With the axis-fold extension, both forms compile to the pairwise tile schedule on CPU, Metal, and CUDA without materializing the full Q × R distance matrix. The published 1.0.0 and post-release comparisons used the nested-map spelling for the explicit implementation. Measured timings, allocations and revision details.

docs.title: Inverse-distance smoothing
docs.text:
Use the same squared distances to predict a scalar observation at each query. Each reference contributes (w, w * value) with w = 1 / (1 + distance²). The compiler computes each score once, sums both fields over each tile, and divides the two totals after the final merge.

Broadcasting NumPyParallel operators 
@parakeet.jit
def smooth_numpy(queries, references, observations):
  observations = observations.reshape(references.shape[0])
  delta = queries[:, None, :] - references[None, :, :]
  weights = 1 / (1 + np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2))
  return np.sum(weights * observations, axis=1) / np.sum(weights, axis=1)

def squared_distance(query, reference):
  return dsl.sum((query - reference) ** dsl.f32(2))



class WeightedSum(NamedTuple):
  weight: dsl.f32
  weighted_value: dsl.f32


def add_sums(left, right):
  return WeightedSum(left.weight + right.weight, left.weighted_value + right.weighted_value)


@dsl.kernel
def smooth_fold(queries, references, observations):
  values = observations.reshape(references.shape[0])
  scores = dsl.allpairs(squared_distance, queries, references)

  def contribution(distance_squared, ref_index):
    weight = 1 / (1 + distance_squared)
    return WeightedSum(weight, weight * values[ref_index])

  def weighted_mean(total):
    return total.weighted_value / total.weight

  return dsl.fold(contribution, add_sums, scores, axis=1, indexed=True, emit=weighted_mean)

docs.text: Train a two-layer transformer to predict the next character in a short text. The complete nanoGPT walkthrough shows the entire runnable program in order, from the first import to the final training step. It follows one input sequence through causal attention, then uses parakeet.map and parakeet.value_and_grad to train on a batch.

docs.title: Gaussian kernel regression
docs.text:
Predict each query's value by weighting reference values by squared distance (Nadaraya-Watson smoothing). The running maximum, weight sum, and weighted output form an associative monoid, so the compiler streams references in tiles instead of allocating an N × M weight matrix. That is the same monoidal reduction at the heart of softmax attention.

@parakeet.jit
def rbf_kernel_regression(x_query, x_train, y_train, neg_gamma):
  d2 = np.sum((x_query[:, None, :] - x_train[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2.0), axis=-1)
  s = d2 * neg_gamma
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ y_train

docs.title: Histograms and tree splits
docs.text:
Accumulate gradients and Hessians into the same bins, take prefix sums, and pick the best split — the core loop of histogram-based gradient boosted trees. When the two scatter-adds share the same bin-index expression, Parakeet fuses them into a single traversal of the observations.

@dsl.kernel
def gbdt_best_split(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Return the split bin with the highest gain and the gain at that bin."""
  g_hist = dsl.scatter(nbins, bin_ids, grads)
  h_hist = dsl.scatter(nbins, bin_ids, hess)
  g_left = dsl.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = dsl.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_tot = g_left[nbins - 1]
  h_tot = h_left[nbins - 1]
  g_right = g_tot - g_left
  h_right = h_tot - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = dsl.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

docs.title: Min-plus matrix product
docs.text:
Replace multiplication with addition and addition with minimum. Each cell takes the shortest two-leg path through an intermediate vertex. Writing the reduction directly over (m, n) and k avoids an m × n × k temporary and triggers the same cache and register tiling as ordinary matrix multiplication.

@dsl.kernel
def tropical_min_plus(a, b):
  """One min-plus matrix product: C[i, j] = min_r (A[i, r] + B[r, j])."""
  m, k = a.shape
  _, n = b.shape
  return dsl.imap(
    lambda i, j: dsl.ireduce(lambda r: a[i, r] + b[r, j], k, combine=dsl.min),
    (m, n),
  )

docs.title: Attention and linear cross-entropy
docs.text:
Both computations normalize scores over a large inner dimension (T keys or V vocabulary entries) and fold them into a much smaller output. Tiling the monoidal reduction avoids materializing the T × T attention matrix or the M × V logit matrix, and the backward pass recomputes score tiles from the inputs instead of saving them on the tape.

Causal attentionLinear cross-entropy 
@parakeet.jit
def causal_flash_attention(q, k, v):
  T = q.shape[-2]
  idx = np.arange(T)
  mask = idx[:, None] >= idx[None, :]
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = np.where(mask, np.matmul(q, np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2)) * scale, np.float32(-1e9))
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return np.matmul(e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True), v)

def cut_cross_entropy(h, w, targets):
  logits = h @ w
  m = np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
  z = logits - m
  lse = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(z), axis=-1))
  picked = z[np.arange(h.shape[0]), targets]
  return -np.mean(picked - lse)

For a sliding window, restrict the mask to keys within the window. When interval analysis proves a whole tile is masked out, the tile is skipped before loading keys or values. See Algebraic laws.

docs.title: Shared keys and compressed attention
docs.text:
Multi-head latent attention writes expanded keys and values as matrix products with a shared low-rank latent c_kv. When the query length is small enough that reassociating the products saves FLOPs, the compiler absorbs w_uk into q and applies w_uv after attention — operating directly on c_kv. Grouped-query attention folds the query-head group into the query tile so shared keys and values are loaded once per group.

Latent attentionGrouped-query attention 
@parakeet.jit
def deepseek_mla(q, c_kv, w_uk, w_uv):
  k = c_kv @ w_uk
  v = c_kv @ w_uv
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = (q @ k.T) * scale
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ v

@parakeet.jit
def gqa_attention(q, k, v):
  # q: (B, H_kv, G, T_q, D), k, v: (B, H_kv, 1, T_kv, D)
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = np.matmul(q, np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2)) * scale
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return np.matmul(e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True), v)

docs.title: Affine scans and state-space models
docs.text:
Two successive affine updates compose into another affine update. That lets Parakeet split a plain Python for t in range(T): recurrence into fixed-size chunks, summarize each chunk in parallel, scan the much shorter sequence of chunk summaries, and finish each chunk independently. The same idea handles both a scalar exponential filter and a matrix-state recurrence.

Scalar IIR filterMamba-2 recurrence 
@parakeet.jit
def iir_exponential_filter(a, b):
  T = a.shape[0]
  out = np.empty_like(b)
  s = np.float32(0.0)
  for t in range(T):
    s = a[t] * s + b[t]
    out[t] = s
  return out

@parakeet.jit
def mamba2_ssd(q, k, v, a):
  T = q.shape[0]
  out = np.empty((T, v.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
  S = np.zeros((k.shape[1], v.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
  for t in range(T):
    S = a[t] * S + k[t][:, None] * v[t][None, :]
    out[t] = q[t] @ S
  return out
