docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Python function + argument types
        │  elaborate (parakeet/frontend/, lib/)
        ▼
 operator IR (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, IndexScatter)
        │  middle-end passes + lowering (parakeet/transforms/)  ──►  f.specialize(x).operators / .ir
        ▼
 typed loop IR (parakeet/syntax/ir.py)
        │  emit C (backends/c.py)            ├─► Metal kernels (backends/metal.py)
        ▼                                    └─► CUDA kernels  (backends/cuda.py)
 system C compiler ─► shared library, cached on disk ─► called through ctypes

docs.title: Specialization
docs.text: Calling a @jit function classifies its arguments — dtype, rank, and layout of arrays, the types of scalars, the structure of tuples/records, and the identity of functions — into a type key. Each distinct key gets one compiled specialization, cached per function. Values read from globals and closures are classified the same way on every call and passed as hidden arguments, so compiled code never sees stale data.

docs.title: Elaboration
docs.text:
The frontend is a staged interpreter: it walks the function's Python AST with an environment of compile-time values and emits IR only for what must happen at run time.

  • Scalars are IR expressions with a NumPy type.
  • Tuples, NamedTuples, fixed-key dicts, frozen dataclasses, slices, functions, closures, and dtypes exist at compile time. Calling a helper function means elaborating its body in place, so by the time IR is produced there are no Python calls, closures, or tuple objects left.
  • Arrays are either concrete (a buffer plus offset, shape, and strides as scalar expressions — slicing is just arithmetic on those) or delayed: a function from index to element. np.tanh(x * a) + b builds a delayed array three layers deep, and no operator is emitted until something consumes it: a store, a reduction, or return. That consumer's operator evaluates the whole expression per element. This handles basic element-wise fusion by construction; larger multi-operator rewrites happen next in the middle end.

Three questions cannot be answered in one forward pass, so elaboration is restarted with what it learned:

  1. the type of a variable modified in a loop (x = 0 then x += 0.5 — restart with x: float);
  2. whether a delayed array must be evaluated eagerly — because it would be evaluated twice, inside a loop, or after an array it reads has been modified (which would change the answer);
  3. which arguments must be compile-time constants (axis=axis), in which case the specialization is additionally keyed on that argument's value.

docs.title: The operator IR
docs.text:
The result of elaboration is a small imperative language: typed scalar variables, flat buffers with load/store, if, counted and unbounded loops, scoped buffer allocation, and runtime checks. On top of it sit five core operator statements, preserving the adverb algebra of the original NYU compiler:

  • IndexMap(shape, index, body): run body for every index; iterations are independent.
  • IndexReduce(shape, index, body, folds): fold the values body computes at every index; each Fold stores its combiner block, an associative primitive name when recognized, and optional multi-state carries. With where, only indices satisfying a predicate participate.
  • IndexFilter(n, index, body, keep): compact the indices where keep holds, in order, into a new array.
  • IndexScan(n, index, body, fold, emit): a running fold; emit runs at every index with the running state.
  • IndexScatter(shape, index, body, dest_size, target, updates): associative index-directed scatter-add (np.bincount, parakeet.scatter_add), supporting multiple fused updates over a shared key.

Tiling passes introduce IndexTile and TileStage nodes on top of the same IR. spec.operators prints a function before the middle-end passes, and spec.ir prints it after lowering. The final pass (transforms/lowering.py) replaces operator statements with loops and with the single parallel construct, ParLoop, which runs its body over chunks of an index range.

Memory management is static: a buffer belongs to the scope that allocated it and is released when that scope ends, unless it escapes into a longer-lived variable, in which case a reference count keeps it alive. Parallel loop bodies never mutate reference counts of shared buffers.

docs.title: Middle-end passes
docs.text:
parakeet/transforms/pipeline.py lists the eleven passes over the operator statements in order (parakeet.transforms.pipeline.names()). Every pass is checked by parakeet.verify when config.verify is enabled, and config.skip_transforms can omit individual passes:

  1. Dead code (simplify.py): removes pure operator statements and unused allocations that nothing reads, to a fixed point.
  2. Normalize (normalize.py): squeezes unit keepdims=True map axes and hoists row-invariant inner reductions (softmax, layer_norm).
  3. Vertical fusion (fusion.py): collapses producer-consumer operator pairs (Map → Map including affine transposes/slices and matmul epilogues, Scan → Map into IndexScan.emit, Map → Filter, Map → Reduce, Map → Scatter) and flattens nested maps.
  4. Filter fusion (fusion.py): merges adjacent IndexFilters into one short-circuiting filter and turns Filter → Reduce into a zero-allocation guarded IndexReduce.
  5. Sibling fusion (fusion.py): merges independent IndexReduces, pure IndexMaps, compatible IndexScatters sharing a key, and online max + sum(exp(x - m)) pairs into single passes.
  6. Contraction reassociation (reassociate.py): reorders chained bilinear contractions when doing so saves FLOPs (including latent-attention absorption).
  7. Monoidal tiling (monoid_tile.py): tiles rescaled semiring reductions (attention, Split-K decoding, linear cross-entropy, Gaussian regression) and applies affine tile-interval mask pruning.
  8. Chunkwise scan (tile_scan.py): rewrites affine and bilinear matrix-state for recurrences into parallel chunkwise scans.
  9. Pairwise fold tiling (pairwise_fold.py): fuses pairwise score producers into ordered tile-summary folds on CPU and GPU (such as exact 1-NN).
  10. Reduction interchange (tiling.py): hoists strided commutative, associative inner reductions outside L1-sized contiguous output strips on CPU (PermuteReductions).
  11. Tiling (tiling.py): rewrites maps wrapping reductions into nested cache/register tiles on CPU and shared-memory tiles on CUDA and Metal.

After those eleven passes, lowering (lowering.py) turns operators into loops and ParLoop chunks.

One transform still runs during elaboration rather than as a middle-end pass:

  • Differentiation (autodiff.py, derivatives.py, algebraic_vjp.py): grad elaborates the function with a tape that records array operators on differentiated values, runs algebraic rematerialization rules (for attention, cross-entropy, and norms), and walks the tape backwards to emit adjoint operators. Scalars differentiate directly from their expression trees, and views map to the same views of their adjoint buffers.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
All targets are C-like, so one emitter (backends/cfamily.py) prints scalar expressions and control flow while backend modules supply target types, math intrinsics, tiled GPU codegen (backends/tiled_gpu.py, backends/monoidal_gpu.py), and runtime error reporting.

  • The host program is always C. Each ParLoop body is outlined into a function taking a context struct (identical bodies up to alpha-renaming share one compiled function) and dispatched through a function pointer supplied at call time — the thread pool, OpenMP, GCD, or a sequential loop — so one compiled library serves every CPU backend.
  • For GPU backends, eligible ParLoops and tiled plans are also emitted as Metal or CUDA kernels. Arrays stay resident on the device across consecutive GPU kernels within a call (and across calls when wrapped with parakeet.to_device).

Scalar helpers (Python/NumPy floor division and modulo, integer powers, shifts, NaN-propagating min/max, and the RNG) live once as C text and are included in the C, Metal, and CUDA preludes so all backends agree bit-for-bit on integer results.

docs.title: Calling convention
docs.text: A compiled entry point takes flat arrays of 64-bit slots: scalars, and for each array its buffer pointer, offset, shape, and strides. Results return the same way. Buffers allocated by compiled code are handed to NumPy without copying using a finalizer that releases the native reference; views of inputs return as NumPy views of the caller's memory.

docs.title: The compiled language
docs.text: Parakeet compiles a subset of Python chosen so that every value has a type known at compile time. This page describes that subset and the places where compiled code deliberately differs from running the same function in CPython.

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text:
Python value Inside compiled code int, float, bool 64-bit integer / double / bool, weakly typed like NumPy treats Python scalars NumPy scalars (np.float32(1), ...) scalars of exactly that dtype NumPy arrays bool, int8–int64, uint8–uint64, float32, float64; any number of dimensions, any strides tuples (also nested) compile-time structures of the above NamedTuples and plain frozen dataclasses fields can hold scalar and array leaves and are accessible by name dictionaries with fixed string keys key order is part of the structure, with lookup by literal key lists, list comprehensions arrays (there are no Python lists in compiled code) None, strings, dtypes, functions, modules compile-time constants slice, range, zip, enumerate supported as values and in loops

float16 data is widened to float32. Complex numbers, object arrays, structured dtypes, general-purpose mutable containers, sets and arbitrary class instances are not supported; passing one raises a TypeError naming the type.

Type promotion follows NumPy 2 (NEP 50) exactly: float32_array * 2.0 stays float32, int8_array + 1 stays int8, int32_array / 2 is float64.

docs.title: Statements
docs.text:
Supported: assignment (including tuple unpacking, augmented and annotated assignment, :=), if/elif/else, for over ranges, arrays, tuples, zip and enumerate, optional else on for and while, break, continue, return anywhere, nested def and lambda, assert, raise of built-in exceptions with a literal message, pass, del.

Not supported: try/except, with, classes, generators (yield), global /nonlocal, import inside a compiled function, f-strings and print. Each of these produces an UnsupportedError at the offending line.

Loop else runs on normal exhaustion, including an empty input. A break skips the corresponding else suite. Strict zip checks lengths at exhaustion. Chained scalar comparisons evaluate each reached operand once and short-circuit.

Unfiltered multi-for comprehensions over independent ranges or arrays compile as Cartesian maps. The rightmost iterator varies fastest. A scalar consumer such as sum(x * y for x in xs for y in ys) can fuse the map into its reduction. Inner iterators with observable setup and dependent domains such as for j in range(i) are outside this subset.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• Any Python function called from compiled code is inlined — helpers do not need @jit. Recursion is therefore not possible and is reported as an error.
  • Positional, keyword, default, keyword-only and *args arguments work; **kwargs does not.
  • Functions are first-class at compile time: pass them as arguments, store them in variables, close over local variables.
  • Globals and closure variables are read on every call, like in Python. If a global changes type, a new specialization is compiled.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Compiled code follows NumPy semantics for views and mutation:

@jit
def f(x):
  v = x[1:]  # a view of the caller's array
  v[0] = 0  # ... so this modifies x
  x += 1  # in place, visible to the caller
  y = x * 2  # a new array
  x[1:] = x[:-1]  # overlapping assignment behaves as if a temporary were made
  return y
  • Basic indexing (x[i, 1:-1, ::2, None, ...]), integer-array indexing and boolean masks work for reading and writing.
  • Indices are bounds-checked (IndexError); shapes are checked when broadcasting (ValueError). Use @jit(bounds_check=False) to drop index checks.
  • Returning an input returns the same object; returning a view of an input returns a NumPy view of the caller's memory.
  • Read-only arrays may be read; writing to one raises ValueError.

docs.title: Differences from CPython / NumPy
docs.text:
One static type per variable : A variable assigned an int on one path and a float on another is a float everywhere (the usual numeric promotion). A function returning 1 in one branch and 2.5 in another returns a float from both. Types that cannot be unified — say an array and None — are an error if the variable is used afterwards.

Rank is static : The number of dimensions of every array is fixed at compile time. Functions whose result rank depends on values (for example np.squeeze(x) when it cannot be known which dimensions have length 1) ask you to pass axis=.

Compile-time constants : Some arguments must be known at compile time: axis, keepdims, the length of a shape tuple, a dtype. If such a value comes straight from an argument of the compiled function, Parakeet specialises on its value automatically; otherwise it reports which expression must be constant.

Lists are arrays : [a, b, c] and [f(x) for x in xs] build arrays. sorted(x) returns an array. There is no append.

Integer arithmetic : Python ints are 64-bit and wrap on overflow (like NumPy), they are not arbitrary precision.

float16 : Operations NumPy would compute in half precision are computed in float32.

Loop variables after a loop : A variable first assigned inside a loop body keeps its last value after the loop, but if the loop never ran it is zero (CPython raises NameError).

Random numbers : np.random functions use Parakeet's own generator (see parakeet.seed); the streams differ from NumPy's.

Parallel side effects : parakeet.map, comprehensions and array expressions may evaluate their elements in parallel and in any order. Reductions with a user-defined function assume it is associative only when Parakeet can prove it (for +, *, min, max, &, |, ^); otherwise they run sequentially.

docs.title: Fixed records at the call boundary
docs.text: Named tuples preserve their field names and result type. Plain frozen dataclasses and dictionaries with fixed string keys can contain arrays or nested records. Fields and keys are part of the specialization, while array data and scalar fields remain ordinary runtime arguments. A dictionary lookup in compiled code requires a known string key. Returning these containers reconstructs their structure and keeps the usual array view semantics.

docs.title: Migrating from Parakeet 0.x
docs.text:
Parakeet 1.0 is a rewrite for Python 3.11+. The decorator and the operators keep their names, and most 0.x programs run after the usual Python 2 → 3 changes (xrange → range, / → // for integer division, print(...)).

0.x 1.0 Python 2.7, dsltools, appdirs Python 3.11+, NumPy 2, nothing else config.backend = "openmp" still works; default is "auto", which needs no OpenMP "llvm" backend removed "interp" backend "python" (runs the original function) "cuda" via PyCUDA + nvcc "cuda" via CuPy, no toolkit install; new "metal" backend f(x, _backend="c") unchanged; also @jit(backend="c") @macro still there, with a different contract: the function gets the compiler and the compile-time values of its arguments instead of syntax nodes (this is how map, reduce and the NumPy functions are defined). @typed_macro and @staged_macro are gone — arguments such as axis are specialised automatically parakeet.testing_helpers parakeet.testing (the old name still imports) config.opt_fusion, config.print_specialized_function, config.print_generated_code still accepted, as aliases of fusion, print_ir and print_code; the other opt_* flags are gone (see Configuration) parakeet.prims.add, parakeet.ndtypes.Int64, Float64, ... unchanged tuple parameters def f((a, b)) not valid Python 3; unpack in the body typed_repr(f, args), specialize(f, args), run_python_fn(f, args) unchanged (also f.specialize(*args).ir) find_broken_transform(fn, inputs, expected) unchanged in spirit: it switches fusion, tiling, the C optimizer and parallel loops on one at a time and names the first that changes the result parakeet.frontend, parakeet.syntax, parakeet.transforms, parakeet.lib the same packages, with new contents: the staged interpreter, the loop IR, and tiling / differentiation parakeet.rank, size, shape, erf, norm, ... unchanged

docs.title: Behaviour changes
docs.text:
• Result types follow NumPy 2. In 0.x bool + bool gave an integer and integer power gave a float; now both give what NumPy gives. Python scalars no longer upcast float32 arrays.
  • Bounds are checked by default. Programs that silently read out of bounds under 0.x now raise IndexError.
  • np.array(x) copies, x += 1 updates in place, views alias — as in NumPy.
  • Globals are read at call time rather than captured at first compilation.
  • parakeet.reduce is parallel only for combiners known to be associative; 0.x assumed associativity for any function.
  • imap(f, shape) passes f a tuple whenever shape is a tuple, including one-element tuples.

docs.title: Data-parallel operators & parakeet.dsl
docs.text:
Parakeet supports two clean, distinct ways to write compiled code over the same algebraic IR:

  1. NumPy frontend (import numpy as np; import parakeet): Decorate ordinary NumPy functions with @parakeet.jit (and use parakeet.grad / parakeet.value_and_grad for differentiation).
  2. Self-contained DSL (from parakeet import dsl): Write explicit data-parallel kernels with @dsl.kernel, dsl.map, dsl.allpairs, dsl.fold, dsl.imap, dsl.ireduce, dsl.scan, dsl.scatter, and dsl.* primitives (dsl.min, dsl.max, dsl.sum, dsl.argmin, dsl.argmax, dsl.exp, dsl.where, dsl.isnan, dsl.f32, dsl.i64, ...) — completely disjoint from NumPy syntax.
from parakeet import dsl
Operator Meaning dsl.map(f, x, y, ..., axis=0) f applied to corresponding slices along axis; axis=None applies it to every scalar element dsl.allpairs(f, x, y, axis=0) result[i, j] = f(x[i], y[j]) dsl.outer_map(f, x, y, z, ...) the n-ary generalisation of allpairs dsl.reduce(f, x, ..., init=None, axis=None, map=None) fold f over all elements, or over slices along axis; with map=g and several arrays, over g(x[i], y[i], ...) dsl.fold(lift, merge, x, init=None, *, axis=None, indexed=False, emit=None) associative structured fold over tuple / NamedTuple states (tiles pairwise folds automatically) dsl.scan(f, x, ..., init=None, axis=0, map=None, emit=None) running fold (a generalised cumsum); emit=h gives h of each running value dsl.imap(f, shape) result[i, j, ...] = f(i, j, ...) for every index of shape (unpacks multi-axis indices automatically; 1-arg tuple lambda ij: also works) dsl.ireduce(f, shape, init=None, combine=dsl.add) reduce f(i, ...) over every index of shape dsl.parfor(f, shape) call f(i, ...) for its side effects, in parallel dsl.filter(pred, x, ..., map=None) the elements of x for which pred is true; with several arrays, map(x[i], y[i], ...) where pred(x[i], y[i], ...) holds dsl.filter_reduce(f, pred, x, ..., map=None, init=None, axis=None) reduce with f over elements where pred holds (fuses into one zero-allocation guarded reduction loop when init is given) dsl.scatter(n, idx, vals) (alias scatter_add) index-directed associative scatter-add (IndexScatter) with thread-privatized parallel lowering and exact gather adjoint dsl.grad(f, argnum=0), dsl.value_and_grad(f, argnum=0) the gradient of a scalar-valued f — see Gradients dsl.show_rewrite(f, *args) inspect which of Parakeet's six algebraic laws rewrote f and view before/after IR 
dsl.map(lambda row: row / dsl.sum(row), X)  # normalise rows
dsl.allpairs(lambda a, b: dsl.sum((a - b) ** dsl.f32(2)), X, C)  # distance matrix
dsl.reduce(dsl.max, X, axis=0)  # column maxima
dsl.imap(lambda i, j: i * 10 + j, (3, 4))  # an index-defined 2D array

dsl.reduce(dsl.add, x, y, map=dsl.mul)  # a dot product; no array of products is built
dsl.scan(dsl.add, x, y, map=lambda a, b: a - b)  # running sum of differences
dsl.filter(lambda a, b: a > b, x, y, map=dsl.add)  # x + y where x > y

For multi-dimensional shapes, imap, ireduce, and parfor unpack coordinates directly when the function takes len(shape) parameters (lambda i, j: ...), and still accept a single index tuple (lambda ij: ...) for backward compatibility. All operators are also available on the top-level parakeet module (e.g. parakeet.map, parakeet.pmap1, parakeet.pmap2).

docs.title: Functions that return arrays
docs.text:
The function given to map may return an array; the results are stacked.

pk.map(lambda row: np.cumsum(row), X)  # shape (n, m)

All results must have the same shape — this is checked at run time (ValueError).

docs.title: Parallelism and associativity
docs.text: map-like operators evaluate elements in parallel, in no particular order. reduce runs in parallel when the combining function is recognisably one of +, *, min, max, and, or, &, |, ^ (whether written as pk.add, np.add or lambda a, b: a + b), and sequentially otherwise — so a non-associative function such as lambda acc, x: acc * 0.5 + x still gives the same answer as functools.reduce. Floating-point sums are reassociated, like NumPy's own pairwise summation: expect differences in the last digits.

docs.title: Primitive functions
docs.text: pk.add, pk.subtract, pk.multiply, pk.divide, pk.minimum, pk.maximum, the comparison and logical/bitwise operators are first-class functions for use with the operators above. Outside compiled code they behave like the NumPy ufuncs of the same name.

docs.title: Structured reductions
docs.text:
dsl.fold(lift, merge, x, init) lifts each axis-0 slice of x to a nonempty tuple or named tuple of scalar fields. The pure merge(left, right) must be associative and return the same field types. Chunks may regroup adjacent values while preserving input order. The initial state is applied once, and is the result for empty input. Read any field of the result in compiled code.

For example, affine updates s -> a*s + b compose in order with merge(left, right) = (right[0]*left[0], right[0]*left[1] + right[1]). Custom folds support forward evaluation. The initial state is optional. With no seed, the first lifted element starts the fold and evaluating an empty lane raises ValueError.

Use axis=k to fold the scalar values along each lane of a multidimensional array. Pass emit=project to return a scalar per lane. With indexed=True, lift(value, index) receives the zero-based position on that axis. The projection runs after the final merge, including on the seed for an empty lane. The gallery composes this operation with allpairs and uses the same score with two different merge rules.

docs.title: Tiled pairwise folds
docs.text:
On CPU, a map over queries can consume an associative structured fold over references whose inputs come from a feature reduction. For example, both the gallery's nested-map 1-NN and the following NumPy expression compile to the same tiled computation:

@pk.jit
def nearest(x, y):
  return np.argmin(np.sum((x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2), axis=2), axis=1)

The compiler evaluates a bounded rectangle of scores, folds each row, and merges consecutive tile summaries in reference order. Each summary carries the global reference index, so ties and NaNs retain their first-index semantics across tiles. The same rewrite handles other pure score reductions, including a sum of absolute differences followed by argmax. The rewrite inspector reports Pairwise map and ordered tile-summary fold when it applies.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Looking for cross-library benchmarks?

For head-to-head 1.0 comparisons against PyTorch, JAX, CuPy, Faiss, and PyKeOps on CPU and an NVIDIA A10, see Release benchmarks. This page explains when and why Parakeet wins or loses on CPUs and GPUs, how cache tiling behaves, and practical tuning tips.

All numbers on this page were measured with python benchmarks/run.py on an Apple M1 Pro (10 cores, 32 GB), macOS 26.5, Python 3.12.6, NumPy 2.5.5; best of five runs, compilation excluded. "NumPy" is the same computation written with NumPy alone; "×" is the speed-up over it. Run the script on your own machine — results vary a lot between CPUs, compilers and array sizes.

docs.title: A big GPU on the work it is for
docs.text:
python benchmarks/gpu_showcase.py on an NVIDIA A100 (Google Colab, 12 CPU threads, float32). The same Python source runs in every column.

kernel size NumPy one core 12 threads A100 A100 vs 12 threads n-body forces 16,384 bodies – 1393 ms 238 ms 7.5 ms 32× k-means assignment 2M points × 256 centers × 16 2247 ms 9551 ms 1913 ms 75.8 ms 25× heat equation, 200 steps 2048² 7821 ms 4532 ms 370 ms 118 ms 3.1× Black-Scholes 20M options 625 ms 1746 ms 227 ms 111 ms 2.0× Julia set 4096² – 1425 ms 155 ms 95.5 ms 1.6×

The first two are what a GPU is for: every element needs thousands of operations and the result is small. The n-body kernel is 186× faster than one core. The last three are bounded by moving their arrays across the bus once each way (Black-Scholes reads 240 MB and writes 80 MB); the heat equation is 600 loops over a grid that never leaves the device between them, which before arrays stayed on the device took 1.4 s here.

A float matrix product is not in this table: on the CPU it goes to the BLAS (24 ms for 2048² on this machine), on the GPU it is Parakeet's own kernel (73 ms). Dense linear algebra on a GPU wants cuBLAS, which Parakeet does not call.

docs.title: Where the GPU starts to win
docs.text:
python benchmarks/crossover.py times the same kernel across sizes. On the same kind of machine (Tesla T4, 2 CPU threads, float32), after tiling and with gradients:

kernel size NumPy one core 2 threads CUDA np.tanh(x * a) + b 100k 0.18 ms 3.3 ms 2.6 ms 0.77 ms 1M 1.7 ms 29.9 ms 30.6 ms 2.8 ms 10M 39.0 ms 277 ms 164 ms 75.5 ms all-pairs distances 1k × 64 9.3 ms 0.42 ms 0.41 ms 0.77 ms 100k × 64 760 ms 34.5 ms 27.3 ms 42.5 ms matrix product 512² 2.5 ms 10.1 ms 8.0 ms 14.3 ms 1024² 24.8 ms 62.3 ms 63.1 ms 49.6 ms 2048² 145 ms 510 ms 654 ms 375 ms Julia set 256² – 5.2 ms 3.0 ms 0.81 ms 1024² – 82.2 ms 47.0 ms 6.4 ms 2048² – 338 ms 197 ms 78.2 ms Harris corners 1024² 9.7 ms 2.9 ms 4.0 ms 3.0 ms 4096² 292 ms 77.0 ms 88.8 ms 133 ms MLP gradient (784-256-10) batch 64 – 3.7 ms 4.1 ms 5.5 ms batch 4096 – 231 ms 189 ms 139 ms decision tree fit (32 features) 100k rows – 4.2 s 3.0 s 2.9 s (CPU)

The GPU wins once each element costs real arithmetic (the Julia set from the smallest size, tanh from about 100k elements) and the result is not much bigger than the work that produced it. It ties or loses when a loop mostly moves memory, because every launch pays for the copy both ways: Harris at 4096² and all-pairs at 100k rows are slower on the device than on two CPU threads. Loops below config.device_threshold (32,768 iterations) never leave the CPU, which is why the decision tree, whose parallel loops run over 32 features, is a CPU program on every backend.

The matrix product is the tiled one: on this machine it is within 2.5–3.5× of NumPy's OpenBLAS on one core.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
Where Parakeet wins. Expressions with several operations (no temporaries, one pass over memory), code that needs a Python-level loop in NumPy (Julia set, GrowCut, pairwise kernels), and anything that can use all cores.

Where it does not.

  • Dense linear algebra, when there is no BLAS to call. A product of two float matrices is handed to the BLAS NumPy itself uses, so it costs what it costs in NumPy. Parakeet's own tiled loops run everything else that has that shape (integer products, allpairs distances, products inside a parallel map or on a GPU) and are 3–10× behind a hand-tuned BLAS.
  • Single-threaded transcendental functions. NumPy ships SIMD implementations of tanh, sin, exp, ...; Parakeet's sequential backend calls the C math library one element at a time (the tanh row). With threads it is ahead again.
  • Memory-bound loops on a GPU. On this machine the 10 CPU cores usually beat the integrated GPU unless each element needs a lot of arithmetic (arc distance, convolution). Loops that mostly move memory (norm, stencils) lose, and repeatedly launching cheap kernels over a NumPy-owned array (diffusion) loses badly because the array is copied to and from the device on every launch.
  • Tiny inputs. A call into compiled code costs a few microseconds of argument marshalling; a NumPy call on a 10-element array is cheaper.

docs.title: Tiling
docs.text:
A matmul-shaped operation is a map over pairs whose element is a reduction over data picked by each member of the pair: a matrix product, allpairs distances, a tropical product. Evaluated row by row, every row of the result sweeps over all of the second operand, which stops fitting in cache long before the arrays are large. Parakeet recognises the shape — any two-dimensional map whose element function is one reduction plus straight-line code, whoever wrote it — and does two things:

  • tiles the inner dimension, so a cache-sized block of the second operand is reused for every row before moving on (config.tile_bytes, by default half of a core's L2 cache);
  • jams the reductions of a 2×4 block of elements into one loop, so each loaded value is used several times.

Neither changes what is computed, only the order. a @ b on 1024×1024 float64 (Apple M1 Max):

one core all cores untiled 190 ms 43 ms tiled 92 ms 13 ms NumPy (Accelerate) 4.5 ms

@jit(tiling=False) or config.tiling = False turns it off. The timings above are with config.blas = False; by default a float matrix product on a CPU backend calls the BLAS and takes the NumPy time.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Prefer array expressions or comprehensions over index loops when they say the same thing: they parallelise, explicit for loops do not.
  • Keep work inside one @jit function so expressions can fuse across helper calls (helpers are inlined automatically).
  • @jit(bounds_check=False) removes index checks from explicit indexing in loops once the code is known to be correct.
  • Compiled code is specialised on whether an input is C-contiguous; contiguous arrays give the C compiler unit strides to vectorise.
  • parakeet.config.fast_math = True allows the C compiler to reorder floating-point arithmetic everywhere (results may change in the last digits).

docs.title: Ideas, history, and boundaries
docs.text:
Parakeet began at New York University in 2012 as a research compiler by Alex Rubinsteyn (@iskandr), with major contributions from Eric Hielscher (@hielscher) and Nathaniel Weinman, guidance from Dennis Shasha, and advice from Russell Power. The original project was hosted at parakeetpython.com and documented in:

  • Alex Rubinsteyn, Runtime Compilation of Array-Oriented Python Programs (PhD thesis, NYU, 2014) — type and value specialization, data-parallel adverbs, and algebraic fusion.
  • Eric Hielscher, Locality Optimization for Data Parallel Programs (PhD thesis, NYU, 2013) — tiling, register blocking, and loop interchange over adverb trees.
  • Papers and talks: HotPar '12 (Parakeet: A Just-In-Time Parallel Accelerator for Python), PyData Boston '13, and PyData NYC '13 (Python on the GPU with Parakeet).

When the original Python 2 codebase was retired, its README left behind a lesson: general Python is the wrong abstraction for high-performance numerical code, and compilers do much better when programs are expressed over a small set of explicit data-parallel operators.

Parakeet 1.0 is a ground-up rewrite for Python 3.11+ and NumPy 2 that tests how far those original ideas can go on modern hardware. It keeps the familiar @jit interface and NumPy frontend, preserves the adverb algebra in its middle end, fixes the soundness gaps noted in the theses, and extends the same machinery to Apple Metal, NVIDIA CUDA, reverse-mode automatic differentiation (grad), and tiled monoidal reductions.

docs.title: 1. Specialize on types and shapes at call time
docs.text:
Python is dynamically typed, yet numerical functions are almost always called with the same dtypes and ranks at a given call site. Parakeet treats your Python function as a template and compiles a native specialization for each distinct combination of argument dtypes, array ranks, memory layouts (contiguous vs. strided), and container structure.

When an expression's type or rank depends on a value — such as axis=, a tuple length, or a unit dimension of length 1 that controls broadcasting — Parakeet specializes on that value automatically. That resolves the broadcasting corner case noted in Rubinsteyn's thesis (200×1 + 1×300) statically at compile time.

docs.title: 2. Lower everything to five data-parallel operators
docs.text:
Instead of maintaining hundreds of hand-written C or GPU kernels for every NumPy function, Parakeet defines array expressions, comprehensions, matrix products, einsum, and user-written adverbs in terms of five operator statements:

  • IndexMap — independent computation over an index space
  • IndexReduce — associative or sequential folds (including multi-carry state such as argmin/argmax and online logsumexp, plus guarded filtered reductions)
  • IndexScan — prefix folds with an optional emit stage
  • IndexFilter — stream compaction of indices matching a predicate
  • IndexScatter — associative index-directed scatter-add (np.bincount, parakeet.scatter_add)

You can inspect a function at this level at any time via f.specialize(*args).operators.

docs.title: 3. Fuse algebraically before lowering to loops
docs.text:
Because programs stay in this small operator IR until the end of the pipeline, optimizations are algebraic identities rather than fragile loop-nest analyses:

  • Vertical fusion collapses producer-consumer chains — map into map (including transposes, slices, stencils, and matmul epilogues like np.tanh(a @ b + c)), map into reduce/scan/filter/scatter, map after scan, filter into filter, and filter into reduce (turning np.sum(x[x > 0]) into one zero-allocation loop).
  • Nested map flattening turns a map inside a map into one multi-dimensional IndexMap, exposing the full index space to CPU threads and GPU grids.
  • Sibling and online fusion lets independent consumers over the same index space share a pass (x.min(), x.max(), np.sin(x), np.cos(x), or sibling histograms with the same bin IDs) and merges dependent max + sum(exp(x - m)) pairs into a single associative pass.
  • Dead-operator elimination drops pure operators and allocations that nothing reads before loops are emitted.

Parakeet 1.0 adds the safety conditions the 2014 thesis omitted: cost and single-use guards so fusion never silently duplicates expensive work, alias checks, and explicit associativity checks so non-associative user folds stay strictly left-to-right.

docs.title: 4. Tile for cache and GPU shared memory from the same IR
docs.text:
Following Hielscher's 2013 thesis, locality transformations operate directly on the operator statements before loop lowering:

  • Reduction interchange hoists strided inner reductions (such as np.sum(X, axis=0)) outside L1-sized strips of contiguous output columns on CPU, while leaving them coalesced across threads on GPU.
  • Invariant hoisting squeezes unit keepdims=True axes and lifts row-level reductions so normalizations like softmax and layer_norm stay L1-resident.
  • Cache, register, and GPU SRAM tiling rewrites maps wrapping reductions (a @ b, allpairs, einsum, tropical products, and fused prologues or epilogues) into nested cache and register tiles on CPU and cooperatively staged shared-memory tiles on CUDA and Metal. On Apple Silicon Metal, float32 contractions use simdgroup_matrix automatically; on CUDA sm_80+, config.tensor_cores=True enables nvcuda::wmma TF32 Tensor Cores.
  • Algebraic laws for modern reductions extend the exact same tiling machinery to rescaled semiring monoids (online softmax, Gaussian kernel regression, attention, cut cross-entropy), contraction reassociation, chunkwise affine/bilinear scans, and tile-interval mask pruning. See Algebraic laws.
  • Persistent GPU residency (parakeet.to_device / to_host) keeps arrays and parameter tuples on CUDA or Metal across calls without repeated host copies.

docs.title: 5. Inspectable, fail-loud compilation
docs.text:
• parakeet.verify checks scoping, types, and buffer ownership before passes, after every pass, and after lowering.
  • f.specialize(*args) exposes .operators, .ir, .source, and .kernels.
  • parakeet.dsl.show_rewrite(f, *args) summarizes which algebraic laws fired.
  • parakeet.find_broken_transform bisects the middle-end passes one by one.
  • Unsupported Python or NumPy features fail at compile time with the exact source caret and inlined call chain instead of silently falling back.

docs.title: What does not work yet
docs.text: Parakeet is a numerical compiler, not a drop-in replacement for all of CPython or SciPy. Knowing the boundary up front avoids surprises.

docs.title: Python language and types
docs.text: Works Not supported yet bool, int8–int64, uint8–uint64, float32, float64 scalars and arrays (any rank or strides) Complex numbers (complex64/complex128), native float16 compute (float16 is widened to float32), structured/record dtypes, object or string arrays Nested tuples, NamedTuples, fixed string-key dicts, plain frozen dataclasses, slice, range, zip, enumerate Dynamic dictionary keys, set, runtime string manipulation, arbitrary user classes and methods List literals and comprehensions as fixed-shape arrays Mutable or dynamically resized Python lists (.append, .extend, ragged lists) if/elif/else, for, while, for/while ... else, break, continue, early return, nested def/lambda, closures, assert, raise try/except, with, generators (yield), global/nonlocal, import inside @jit, **kwargs, recursion Static array rank; compile-time specialization on axis, keepdims, dtype, tuple lengths Value-dependent output rank (e.g. np.squeeze(x) without axis=), variables whose types cannot unify

docs.title: NumPy and SciPy coverage
docs.text:
About 200 core NumPy functions and ufuncs are built in (see Supported functions), covering arithmetic, reductions, scans, sorting, masks and fancy indexing, @/dot/einsum, np.linalg.norm, and parallel np.random. Not yet built in:

  • Matrix decompositions and solvers (np.linalg.svd, solve, inv, eig, cholesky, qr, det, lstsq)
  • Spectral transforms (np.fft.*)
  • Variable-cardinality set operations (np.unique, np.lexsort, np.isin)
  • SciPy modules (scipy.special, scipy.optimize, scipy.ndimage, ...)

docs.title: Automatic differentiation (grad / value_and_grad)
docs.text:
grad differentiates element-wise operations, reductions (sum, zero-safe prod, min, max, general folds), cumsum, sort, @, einsum, views and concatenation, gather and scatter_add, map/allpairs with user functions, and pure runtime if branches — enough to train small transformers (examples/nanogpt.py) and convnets (examples/convnet.py). Current boundaries:

  • Elaboration-time tape: differentiation records operators during elaboration (with an algebraic tape optimizer for attention, cross-entropy, and norms) rather than running as an IR-to-IR pass over lowered operators.
  • No dynamic-length loops over differentiated values: for loops with a compile-time-known length (up to 4,096) unroll and differentiate; while loops or loops over runtime array lengths are refused (rewrite with reduce, map, or scan).
  • Pure runtime if branches only: both branches execute and are selected by the condition, so branches touching differentiated values cannot contain array stores, return, break, or raise.
  • Missing derivative rules (refused loudly): cumprod, convolve, user-defined scan combiners, in-place indexed assignment (out[idx] = v; use parakeet.scatter_add or np.bincount(..., weights=w) instead), and overwriting an array still needed by an earlier backward rule.
  • Second derivatives: work through element-wise ops, reductions, @, and views; not yet through map, gather indexing, or cumsum.

docs.title: GPU and locality boundaries
docs.text:
• Apple Metal has no hardware float64: float64 loops fall back to CPU cores with a warning; use float32 on Metal.
  • No per-thread heap allocation on GPU: a parallel loop that allocates temporary arrays or selects between buffer aliases inside its body runs on CPU instead of CUDA or Metal.
  • Dense GEMM vs. cuBLAS: CPU backends call NumPy's BLAS for standalone float A @ B. GPU backends run Parakeet's own shared-memory tiled kernels (including Metal simdgroup_matrix and optional CUDA TF32 WMMA), which fuse prologues and epilogues in one kernel but trail hand-tuned cuBLAS on large standalone matrix multiplies.
  • Analytical tile sizing: tile sizes are picked analytically from target cache and shared-memory budgets (config.tile_bytes) rather than Hielscher's online runtime search. Chunkwise TileScan handles affine and bilinear recurrences; general cache-tiled TiledScan for arbitrary scans is not implemented.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or newer and NumPy 2.
  • A C compiler: the Xcode command line tools on macOS (xcode-select --install), gcc or clang on Linux, MinGW-w64 gcc or LLVM clang on Windows.

Install Parakeet in your environment (or python -m pip install . in a local checkout):

pip install parakeet
python -c "import parakeet; print(parakeet.available_backends())"

available_backends() reports, for every backend, either "ok" or the reason it cannot be used on this machine and how to fix it.

docs.title: Your first compiled function
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from parakeet import jit


@jit
def rms(x):
  return np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x))


x = np.random.rand(1_000_000)
rms(x)  # first call: compiles for (float64 array, 1-d), then runs
rms(x)  # later calls: straight into native code
rms(x.astype(np.float32))  # a new specialization, compiled on demand

Compilation takes a few hundred milliseconds per specialization (most of it in the C compiler) and is cached on disk, so a second run of your program starts fast.

jit also works without decorator syntax, including on lambdas and NumPy functions:

fast_rms = jit(lambda x: np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x)))
parakeet.run(rms.fn, x)  # compile-and-call in one step

docs.title: Loops, comprehensions, helpers
docs.text:
Anything in the supported subset can be mixed freely. Helper functions are inlined automatically — they do not need their own @jit.

def sqr_dist(a, b):
  return np.sum((a - b) ** 2)


@jit
def nearest(X, centroids):
  return np.array([np.argmin([sqr_dist(x, c) for c in centroids]) for x in X])

You can also call Parakeet's data-parallel operators directly (parakeet.map, reduce, scan, allpairs, scatter_add, dsl.fold) when you want to apply a Python function over slices or pairs in parallel. See Data-parallel operators.

docs.title: Gradients in one line
docs.text:
Wrap any scalar-valued function with parakeet.grad or parakeet.value_and_grad. The forward and backward passes compile together into one native function:

from parakeet import value_and_grad


def mse_loss(w, x, y):
  return np.mean((np.tanh(x @ w) - y) ** 2)


loss_val, dw = value_and_grad(mse_loss)(w, x, y)

See Gradients for nested parameter tuples, NamedTuples, frozen dataclasses, and training loops.

docs.title: Picking a backend
docs.text:
@jit(backend="metal")  # per function
def f(x): ...


f(x, _backend="c")  # per call
parakeet.config.backend = "threads"  # process-wide
with parakeet.options(backend="c", num_threads=1):  # temporarily
  f(x)

See Backends and GPUs for multi-core tuning, Metal, CUDA, and keeping arrays resident on a GPU with parakeet.to_device.

docs.title: Looking inside
docs.text:
spec = rms.specialize(x)  # compile without running
print(spec.operators)  # high-level operator IR before middle-end passes
print(spec.ir)  # typed, fused loop IR
print(spec.source)  # generated C

def rms(x_1: array[float64, 1d]):
    nchunks_9: int64? = @num_chunks(x_n0_3, True)
    partials_10 = alloc(float64, nchunks_9)
    parallel[reduce] for chunk_11, (start_12, stop_13) in chunks(x_n0_3, n=nchunks_9):
        x_15: float64 = (x_1[(x_off_2 + start_12)] * x_1[(x_off_2 + start_12)])
        acc_14: float64 = x_15
        for i_16 in range((start_12 + 1), stop_13, 1):  # simd
            x_17: float64 = (x_1[(x_off_2 + i_16)] * x_1[(x_off_2 + i_16)])
            acc_14: float64 = (acc_14 + x_17)
        partials_10[chunk_11] = acc_14
    acc_8: float64 = 0.0
    for i_18 in range(0, nchunks_9, 1):
        acc_8: float64 = (acc_8 + partials_10[i_18])
    red_19: float64 = acc_8
    res_20: float64 = sqrt((red_19 / float64(x_n0_3)))
    return res_20

No temporary for x * x exists: the multiplication was fused into the parallel reduction. To see a high-level summary of which algebraic rewrites fired on a function, call parakeet.dsl.show_rewrite(fn, *example_args).summary().

docs.title: When something is not supported
docs.text:
You get a CompileError pointing at your code, not a crash:

parakeet.errors.UnsupportedError: numpy.fft.fft is not supported in compiled code
  File "demo.py", line 6, in spectrum
    return np.fft.fft(x)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Run the function uncompiled at any time with backend="python" to separate a bug in your code from a limitation of the compiler. More in Errors and debugging.

docs.title: Rewrite rules and optimizations
docs.text:
Everything Parakeet does to a program between your source and the loops it runs, in one place, and how that compares with the two theses that describe the original system:

  • [R] Alex Rubinsteyn, Runtime Compilation of Array-Oriented Python Programs (NYU, 2014) — the operators and their fusion rules.
  • [H] Eric Hielscher, Locality Optimization for Data Parallel Programs (NYU, 2013) — tiling.

The short version: the rules are the same algebra, applied in two places.

  • While elaborating. An array expression is a delayed value — a function from index to element — and the vertical fusion rules fire at the moment an operator is applied to one. F ∘ G below means "the element function of the result is F applied to the element function of the argument"; no pass looks for the pattern afterwards.
  • In the middle end. Elaboration produces the original compiler's indexified level: operator statements (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, and IndexScatter) over index spaces with ordinary scalar bodies (Specialization.operators prints it). Middle-end passes rewrite those statements in order: dead code elimination, normalization, vertical fusion (exact and affine map/scan/filter/reduce/scatter), filter fusion, sibling and online monoidal fusion, bilinear contraction reassociation (Law 3), monoidal tiling and tile-interval pruning (Laws 1 & 5), chunkwise affine/bilinear scans (Law 4), pairwise fold tiling, reduction interchange, and cache/register/GPU tiling. A final pass (LowerAdverbs in spirit) lowers operators into loops. parakeet.transforms.pipeline.PASSES is the authoritative list, and find_broken_transform toggles its passes on one at a time. See Algebraic laws for the mathematical identities behind these passes and the Kernel gallery for runnable examples.

[R] §4.6 here Map(f, X1..Xn, axis) map(f, x1, ..., xn, axis=0), each; axis=None for every scalar OuterMap(f, X1..Xn, axis) outer_map(f, x1, ..., xn), allpairs(f, x, y) IndexMap(f, shape) imap(f, shape) Reduce(f, ⊕, X1..Xn, init, axis) reduce(⊕, x1, ..., xn, map=f, init=, axis=) IndexReduce(f, ⊕, shape) ireduce(f, shape, init=, combine=⊕) Scan(f, ⊕, emit, X1..Xn, init, axis) scan(⊕, x1, ..., xn, map=f, emit=, init=, axis=) Filter(f, pred, X1..Xn) filter(pred, x1, ..., xn, map=f) ParFor(f, bounds) parfor(f, bounds) IndexFilter(pred, shape) what x[mask], np.nonzero and filter are built on: an IndexFilter statement FilterReduce, IndexFilterReduce filter_reduce(⊕, pred, x1, ..., xn, map=, init=, axis=) — and any reduction over a filter also becomes one (see fusion) IndexScan(f, ⊕, emit, shape) what scan, np.cumsum and np.cumprod are built on: an IndexScan statement, whose emit is a block (it stores the running value) — IndexScatter (parakeet.scatter_add, np.bincount): index-directed associative scatter-add with thread-privatized parallel lowering and exact gather adjoint — grad(f), value_and_grad(f)

Every NumPy function is defined in terms of these: np.sum is a reduce, np.cumsum a scan, a @ b and np.einsum a map of reductions, a comprehension an imap.

docs.title: Vertical: a producer into its consumer
docs.text:
rule ([R] Fig. 6.1) status Map(g, Map(f, X)) ⇒ Map(g∘f, X) yes — including affine coordinate inversion (AffineInlineBufferLoad) for transpose, shifted-slice, and stencil fusion, plus cost-bounded multi-consumer fusion Map(g, IndexMap(f, σ)) ⇒ IndexMap(g∘f, σ) yes OuterMap(g, Map(f, X1), X2..) ⇒ OuterMap(λ. g(f(x1), x2..), X1..) yes Reduce(g, ⊕, Map(f, X)) ⇒ Reduce(g∘f, ⊕, X) yes Reduce(g, ⊕, IndexMap(f, σ)) ⇒ IndexReduce(g∘f, ⊕, σ) yes Scatter(⊕, idx, Map(f, X)) ⇒ IndexScatter(⊕, idx, f(X)) yes (transforms/fusion.py): elementwise weight maps fuse directly into np.bincount / parakeet.scatter_add Scan(g, ⊕, ε, Map(f, X)) ⇒ Scan(g∘f, ⊕, ε, X) yes Filter(g, pred, Map(f, X)) ⇒ Filter(g∘f, pred∘f, X) yes: the predicate and the kept values both read the unfused map Map(g, Filter(f, pred, X)) ⇒ Filter(g∘f, pred, X) yes: the selected elements are a delayed gather that the map fuses into Map(g, Scan(f, ⊕, ε, X)) ⇒ Scan(f, ⊕, g∘ε, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): a consumer IndexMap whose single input is an IndexScan's output fuses into the scan's emit block (np.cumsum(x) * 2.0 + 1.0 runs in one scan pass) Reduce(g, ⊕, Filter(f, p, X)) ⇒ FilterReduce(g∘f, ⊕, p, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): becomes a guarded IndexReduce with no index array (see below) Filter(g, p2, Filter(f, p1, X)) ⇒ Filter(g∘f, p1 ∧ (p2∘f), X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): short-circuiting single compaction, which also feeds into FilterReduce

Side conditions. [R] states one: nothing may modify the intermediate array between producer and consumer, decided by alias analysis. Here every delayed array records how many stores had happened when it was created; if a store that may alias what it reads has happened by the time it is consumed, elaboration restarts with that expression evaluated eagerly where it was written.

[R] states no condition on how often the intermediate is used, so fusing could duplicate work. Here a delayed array that costs more than a few operations per element may be consumed once; a second consumer, or a consumer inside a loop, triggers the same restart. That is the main correction to the thesis's rules.

docs.title: Nested: a map of maps
docs.text:
rule ([R] Fig. 6.2) status Map(λxi. Map(f, xi), x) ⇒ Map(f, x) yes, when the inner map is cheap and its shape does not depend on xi: the result is one delayed array over the whole index space Map(λxi. Map(f, y), x) ⇒ OuterMap(f, x, y) yes, same condition IndexMap(λi. IndexMap(f, σ2), σ1) ⇒ IndexMap(f, σ1 ++ σ2) yes, same condition

When the inner map is expensive, elaboration emits a nested IndexMap writing directly into its row of one output array (no per-row allocation), and the middle-end vertical fusion pass (CombineNestedMaps) flattens it into a single multi-dimensional IndexMap whenever the inner shape does not depend on the outer index — exposing the full 2D/ND index space to multi-core CPUs and GPUs.

docs.title: Horizontal: two consumers of one array
docs.text:
rule ([R] Fig. 6.3) status a = Reduce(f, ⊕1, X); b = Reduce(g, ⊕2, X) ⇒ a, b = Reduce(f×g, ⊕1×⊕2, X) yes, as sibling fusion (transforms/fusion.py): two IndexReduce statements over the same index space, the second not using the first's result, become one statement with two folds. x.min(), x.max() reads x once a = Map(f, X); b = Map(g, X) ⇒ a, b = Map(f×g, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): two pure IndexMap statements over the same index space where the second does not read what the first writes share one loop (np.sin(x), np.cos(x) reads x once)

Conditions the thesis leaves out: the index spaces must be provably equal (the same expression once shape variables are resolved), both seeded or both unseeded, and both must stay vectorizable — a float sum is not fused with a max, which would cost the sum its SIMD loop. Scalar definitions between the two statements are stepped over when they do not use the first result.

Tiling (below) uses the same rule on copies of one reduction.

docs.title: Filter fusion
docs.text:
rule ([R] Fig. 6.1) status Reduce(g, ⊕, Filter(f, p, X)) ⇒ FilterReduce(g ∘ f, ⊕, p, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): an IndexFilter followed by an IndexReduce over what it kept becomes one guarded IndexReduce over the filter's own index space. np.sum(x[x > 0]) is one parallel loop and allocates nothing (about 3× faster on 5M elements) Filter(q, Filter(p, X)) ⇒ Filter(p ∧ q, X) yes (transforms/fusion.py): adjacent IndexFilter statements where the second filters the first's survivors collapse into one short-circuiting IndexFilter (and if reduced afterwards, into one FilterReduce) Map(f, Filter(p, X)) ⇒ one loop half: the map is a delayed array over the kept indices, so it fuses with its consumer (or directly into FilterReduce) but a returned filter still compacts first

Conditions: nothing else reads the kept indices (returning x[mask] keeps the filter); the reduction has an init, because the first element may not survive (np.min(x[mask]) stays two steps so that an empty selection still raises); it runs in parallel only when every fold has an identity to start a chunk from. If the number of survivors is used (np.mean), counting it is one more fold. Inside the fused loop the bounds check on the gathered index is dropped: the index is the loop's own.

docs.title: Reductions and scans
docs.text:
• Associativity. [R] calls the combiner "commutative" and never requires associativity; [H] requires both. Here a fold is regrouped (run in chunks, vectorized) only when its combiner is recognisably one of + * min max and or & | ^, however it was written (np.add, lambda a, b: a + b). Any other function is folded strictly left to right.
  • Several axes at once. Reduce over axes A of X ⇒ a map over the other axes of one reduction over a block: the reduced axes are moved last (a view) and each block is folded in a single pass.
  • A reduction with carried state (Carry). argmin/argmax fold (value, index) pairs per chunk and combine the pairs in index order, so the first of equal elements still wins. The same Fold.carries monoid machinery also fuses dependent m = max(x); s = sum(exp(x - m)) pairs into a single parallel associative (m, s) pass (fuse_online_logsumexp) for 1-pass logsumexp and zero-temp softmax.
  • Parallel scan. Scan(⊕, X) with an associative primitive ⇒ fold every chunk; prefix the chunk totals; scan every chunk from its prefix.
  • Parallel filter. X[mask] ⇒ count per chunk; prefix the counts; every chunk writes its survivors from its own offset.

docs.title: Linear algebra
docs.text:
• a @ b ⇒ Map((i, j) ↦ Reduce(+, a[i, :] * b[:, j])): a map of reductions like any other, so it fuses with what feeds it.
  • Layout. The inner loop should walk both operands with stride one: b is replaced by its transpose copied once, unless it is already the transpose of a contiguous array, and transpose(transpose(x)) ⇒ x.
  • Stacks. A @ B with B a matrix ⇒ reshape the stack to one tall matrix, one product, reshape back.
  • Einstein summation. einsum(spec, X1..Xn) ⇒ view every operand in one index space (output labels, then summed labels), multiply element-wise, reduce the trailing block. 'ij,jk->ik' exactly ⇒ @.
  • BLAS. A product of two float matrices outside a parallel loop ⇒ cblas_?gemm from the library NumPy itself uses, with the transpose flags set for transposed views. (config.blas = False keeps the generated loops.)

docs.title: Scalars and shapes
docs.text:
Done while expressions are built; there is no simplification pass:

  • constant folding with NumPy's semantics;
  • x + 0, x - 0, x * 1, x // 1 ⇒ x and x * 0 ⇒ 0 for integers (not floats: -0.0 and nan); select(c, a, b) with constant c; not not x; and/or with a constant side;
  • x ** 2 ⇒ x * x, x ** 0.5 ⇒ sqrt(x), x ** 1 ⇒ x;
  • a slice of a slice, a transpose, a reshape of a contiguous array, an expand_dims are arithmetic on offset and strides: no copy, no loop;
  • dimensions proven equal (by a broadcast check that already ran) are not checked again; an index known to be within its loop's bound gets no bounds check.

Specialization on values ([R] ch. 6.6 partially evaluates on inputs equal to 0 or 1). Here: a dimension of length 1 is always a constant (which is what makes broadcasting static — [R] lists 200x1 + 1x300 as giving a wrong answer); a scalar argument or an array dimension becomes a constant when the code needs one (axis=, the length of a tuple, a loop that has to be unrolled).

Left to the C compiler, which does them well on the loops it is given: common subexpressions, dead code, loop-invariant code motion, scalar replacement, unrolling, vectorization. [R]'s pipeline did these itself, on its own IR.

docs.title: Parallelism and placement
docs.text:
• Every map, reduction, scan, filter and parfor is a parallel loop over chunks; a parallel loop inside another is a sequential one.
  • A loop goes to the GPU when elements × estimated inner iterations per element reaches config.device_threshold: a short loop over long rows goes, a long loop of cheap elements below the threshold does not.
  • Between the loops of one call, arrays stay on the device. Host code that reads or writes array memory itself asks for the device's copies first.

  • Its own low-level optimizer (it relies on the C compiler instead).

docs.title: Train nanoGPT from scratch
docs.text:
This character-level GPT learns to predict the next character in a short passage. For the fragment para, one training sequence has inputs p a r and targets a r a. At the second position, the model can see p a and must predict r. A causal mask enforces that rule even though the model computes predictions for every position at once.

The six Python blocks below make one complete file. You can copy them in order into train_gpt.py and run python train_gpt.py, or run the same file from the repository. To run the repository version, use Python 3.11 or newer and a C compiler.

git clone https://github.com/iskandr/parakeet.git
cd parakeet
python -m pip install -e .
python -m examples.nanogpt

The text is embedded in the script. The default run trains on batches of 16 sequences, each 32 characters long, for 60 steps.

docs.title: Normalize one position at a time
docs.text:
One input sequence becomes a matrix of shape (context, width). Each row holds one character's embedding. layer_norm normalizes across the features of that row. Later, each row passed to softmax contains the attention scores from one position to every position in the sequence. Subtracting the row maximum keeps the exponential stable.

"""A character-level GPT trained with parakeet.value_and_grad.

The model is a function over a tuple of parameter arrays: token and position
embeddings, a stack of pre-norm transformer blocks (causal self-attention and
an MLP), and a linear head.  ``value_and_grad`` differentiates the loss of a
batch with respect to all of them, and plain Python applies Adam.
"""

import time

import numpy as np

import parakeet

N_HEAD = 2


def layer_norm(x, gain, bias):
  mu = np.mean(x, axis=1, keepdims=True)
  var = np.mean((x - mu) ** 2, axis=1, keepdims=True)
  return (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + 1e-5) * gain + bias


def softmax(x):
  e = np.exp(x - np.max(x, axis=1, keepdims=True))
  return e / np.sum(e, axis=1, keepdims=True)

docs.title: Mix information across visible characters
docs.text:
Each attention head uses part of the model width. For each position, q represents what it is looking for, k what each position can match, and v what that position contributes. Their score matrix has shape (context, context). In the para example, row two may give weight to the first two inputs. The mask suppresses the score of the third before softmax.

The heads contribute to a shared output through wo. A transformer block adds this attention output back to its input. It then applies a two-layer network to each position and adds that result back too.

def attention(x, wq, wk, wv, wo, causal):
  """Causal self-attention over one sequence: x is (T, C)."""
  head_width = x.shape[1] // N_HEAD
  q, k, v = x @ wq, x @ wk, x @ wv
  out = x * 0.0
  for h in range(N_HEAD):
    lo, hi = h * head_width, (h + 1) * head_width
    scores = q[:, lo:hi] @ k[:, lo:hi].T / np.sqrt(head_width)
    weights = softmax(np.where(causal, scores, -1e9))
    # Add this head’s contribution to the output embedding.
    out = out + (weights @ v[:, lo:hi]) @ wo[lo:hi]
  return out


def block(x, p, causal):
  g1, b1, wq, wk, wv, wo, g2, b2, w1, c1, w2, c2 = p
  x = x + attention(layer_norm(x, g1, b1), wq, wk, wv, wo, causal)
  h = np.tanh(layer_norm(x, g2, b2) @ w1 + c1)
  return x + h @ w2 + c2

docs.title: Score one sequence, then a batch
docs.text:
wte[tokens] looks up one embedding per character ID. Adding wpe gives each position its own embedding as well. After the transformer blocks, the output matrix head maps each position to one score per character in the vocabulary. sequence_loss converts those scores to log probabilities, picks the entry for the actual next character at each position, and averages the negative values.

In loss, both tokens and targets have shape (batch, context). The two arguments to loss_for_sequence are matching rows, and every sequence shares the same params and causal mask. parakeet.map maps loss_for_sequence across the batch to produce one scalar loss per sequence, and np.mean averages them into the batch loss. parakeet.value_and_grad(loss) compiles a function returning both that scalar loss and its gradient with respect to params (the first argument of loss).

def sequence_loss(params, tokens, targets, causal):
  wte, wpe, blocks, gf, bf, head = params
  x = wte[tokens] + wpe
  for p in blocks:
    x = block(x, p, causal)
  logits = layer_norm(x, gf, bf) @ head
  z = logits - np.max(logits, axis=1, keepdims=True)
  logp = z - np.log(np.sum(np.exp(z), axis=1, keepdims=True))
  return -np.mean(logp[np.arange(len(targets)), targets])


def loss(params, tokens, targets, causal):
  def loss_for_sequence(input_ids, next_ids):
    return sequence_loss(params, input_ids, next_ids, causal)

  per_sequence = parakeet.map(loss_for_sequence, tokens, targets)
  return np.mean(per_sequence)


loss_and_grad = parakeet.value_and_grad(loss)

docs.title: Build the parameter arrays
docs.text:
init constructs the tuple that sequence_loss unpacks. In order, it contains the token embedding table, the position embedding table, the tuple of transformer blocks, the final normalization gain and bias, and the output matrix. With the defaults, the token embedding table has shape (vocab, 32) and the output matrix has shape (32, vocab).

Inside one_block, the first gain and bias normalize the input to attention. The next four matrices project queries, keys, values and the combined output. A second gain and bias precede the two weight–bias pairs of the position-wise network. This is the order in which block unpacks them.

def init(vocab, context, width, layers, rng):
  def w(*shape):
    return rng.normal(0.0, 0.02, shape)

  def one_block():
    ones, zeros = np.ones(width), np.zeros(width)
    return (
      ones, zeros, w(width, width), w(width, width), w(width, width), w(width, width),
      ones.copy(), zeros.copy(), w(width, 4 * width), np.zeros(4 * width), w(4 * width, width), zeros.copy(),
    )  # fmt: skip

  blocks = tuple(one_block() for _ in range(layers))
  return (w(vocab, width), w(context, width), blocks, np.ones(width), np.zeros(width), w(width, vocab))

docs.title: Update every parameter with Adam
docs.text:
A call to loss_and_grad returns the batch loss and a gradient array for each parameter array. The gradients follow the same nested tuple structure as the parameters. tree_map walks corresponding leaves together so Adam can update an embedding, a bias or a projection matrix with the same formula. m tracks a moving average of the gradients and v tracks a moving average of their squares. Both travel with the parameters into the next step.

def tree_map(f, *trees):
  if isinstance(trees[0], tuple):
    return tuple(tree_map(f, *parts) for parts in zip(*trees))
  return f(*trees)


def adam(params, grads, m, v, step, lr=3e-3, b1=0.9, b2=0.99):
  m = tree_map(lambda m, g: b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g, m, grads)
  v = tree_map(lambda v, g: b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g * g, v, grads)
  scale = lr * np.sqrt(1 - b2**step) / (1 - b1**step)
  params = tree_map(lambda p, m, v: p - scale * m / (np.sqrt(v) + 1e-8), params, m, v)
  return params, m, v


def train_step(params, m, v, step, tokens, targets, causal):
  value, grads = loss_and_grad(params, tokens, targets, causal)
  params, m, v = adam(params, grads, m, v, step)
  return value, params, m, v

docs.title: Train on shifted character windows
docs.text:
main assigns one integer ID to each distinct character in TEXT. For a sample starting at offset i, tokens starts at i and targets starts at i + 1. Stacking those windows gives the two arrays consumed by the batch map. The lower triangle of causal includes the diagonal, so a position can read its own input when predicting the following character.

TEXT = (
  "parakeet compiles numerical python. it fuses array expressions into loops, "
  "runs them on every core, and now differentiates them too. "
) * 8


def main(steps=60, batch=16, context=32, width=32, layers=2, seed=0, verbose=False):
  rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
  chars = sorted(set(TEXT))
  data = np.array([chars.index(c) for c in TEXT])
  params = init(len(chars), context, width, layers, rng)
  m = tree_map(np.zeros_like, params)
  v = tree_map(np.zeros_like, params)
  causal = np.tril(np.ones((context, context))) > 0
  first = last = None
  start = time.perf_counter()
  for step in range(1, steps + 1):
    at = rng.integers(0, len(data) - context - 1, batch)
    tokens = np.stack([data[i : i + context] for i in at])
    targets = np.stack([data[i + 1 : i + context + 1] for i in at])
    value, params, m, v = train_step(params, m, v, step, tokens, targets, causal)
    first = value if first is None else first
    last = value
    if verbose and (step == 1 or step % 20 == 0):
      print(f"step {step:3d}  loss {value:.3f}  ({time.perf_counter() - start:.1f}s)")
  assert last < 0.8 * first, (first, last)
  return first, last


if __name__ == "__main__":
  main(verbose=True)

The first training step compiles the forward and gradient kernels; subsequent steps reuse the compiled native code. With --verbose (the default when run as a script), main prints the cross-entropy loss at steps 1, 20, 40, and 60 and asserts that training makes progress (final loss below 80% of step 1). Using the fixed seed=0 above, the printed loss drops from 3.173 at step 1 to 2.307 (step 20), 1.796 (step 40), and 1.250 (step 60) on GPU (with nearly identical values on CPU).

For larger four-head training runs where the Adam update is also compiled into the training step, see the nanoGPT training benchmark. The compact two-head walkthrough above keeps Adam in plain Python so every line is easy to follow.
